groups.question: Why does the body need carbon dioxide?
texts:
You mostly just can't get rid of it. Every cell you've got is making the stuff as a waste product of burning glucose for energy. You end up with a lot of it in the blood, and that accidentally keeps your pH from crashing. Most of it gets parked there as bicarbonate, which is the main thing stopping your blood from getting too acidic. Knock that out and you'd have a really hard time keeping your chemistry in any sort of working order. That same buildup is what your brain uses to keep the local blood flow up, too. So you are sort of dependent on the thing you are constantly trying to get rid of.

You'd be in pretty bad shape if you did manage to scrub your whole system down to zero. Get most of it out and the buffer system just stops working. You don't have to take in any of it from the outside to get any of those benefits, either. You are always making plenty of it for free.

It's mostly a matter of you getting rid of it. Every cell you have is burning oxygen and making CO2 as a byproduct, and that stuff has to go somewhere. If it piled up in the blood the whole thing would turn far too acidic to keep working. The body got around that by letting CO2 dissolve into water and become bicarbonate. That bicarbonate ends up doing most of the heavy lifting to keep your blood pH in a workable range. You'd lose almost all of that buffering capacity if you somehow got rid of the CO2.

It also happens to be the thing your brain uses to keep a proper rate of blood flow. The little vessels in the cerebral cortex widen or narrow pretty much in response to the local CO2 concentration. This is why hyperventilating makes you feel lightheaded. You've blown off enough of the gas to have those vessels clamp down too far. So you are stuck with a waste product that has ended up being load bearing in a couple of other ways.

You get a little of it from every cell that burns sugar for energy so it's always hanging around. That constant supply turns out to be pretty handy. Most of the bicarbonate floating in your blood is just that CO2 that has picked up a water molecule. The two of them keep your blood from getting too acidic or too basic. You'd be in pretty rough shape without that buffer.

Your brain also keeps a very close eye on the CO2 level to keep you breathing at the right rate. That's why you end up feeling lightheaded if you take a bunch of fast deep breaths. You've flushed out too much and the whole system gets thrown off. That lightheadedness is your brain trying to get you to slow down.

You can get by on a little but you can't do without it. You'd just end up with a blood chemistry that your cells can't function in.

You are mostly right to think of it as a waste product, the cells just dump it out. The trouble is that the plumbing for getting rid of it ends up doing a few other necessary jobs. Most of your blood acid gets mopped up by turning that CO2 into bicarbonate. Without it the whole thing gets far more acidic than your organs can stand. You also need a certain amount of the gas stuck to your hemoglobin to get the oxygen off in the first place. Change the CO2 level and you change how easily the hemoglobin lets go of that oxygen.

Your brain has a separate and fairly sensitive gauge for it as well. It watches the CO2 level and uses that to set your breathing rate. You can have plenty of oxygen and still feel you are suffocating if that gauge reads wrong. Breathe into a paper bag and you are just recycling your own gas to quiet the alarm, you aren't actually putting more oxygen into your blood.

It's mostly a matter of keeping your blood from getting too alkaline. You've got this whole buffering system in there that runs on a carbonic acid and bicarbonate pair, and the CO2 is what keeps that pair in balance. Get rid of too much and you end up with respiratory alkalosis, which messes with just about every enzyme you've got.

It also helps get oxygen where it needs to go. Hemoglobin holds onto that oxygen a lot more tightly when there isn't much CO2 around. That's called the Bohr effect and it's the whole reason you don't suffocate in your own tissues. Since you are making the stuff off all the time from your own cell respiration, the only thing you really have to get right is your breathing rate.

It's mostly a matter of keeping your blood from getting too alkaline. Your red blood cells swap CO2 for a hydrogen ion to keep the pH in a narrow range and you'd get into pretty bad trouble if that didn't happen. You also can't get rid of the hydrogen ions the kidneys have to deal with without having some CO2 on hand. On top of that hemoglobin won't let go of its oxygen very well unless CO2 is around to get it to. You feel the need to breathe long before you've run short on oxygen because your brain is reading the CO2 level.

That said you aren't "needing" it in the way you need food. You are mostly stuck with it as the unavoidable by product of cells making the energy you actually do need.

It's mostly that the blood needs it to keep from getting too acidic. Your cells dump it out as a waste product and the blood picks it up and turns most of that into bicarbonate. That bicarbonate acts as a buffer to stop the whole thing from swinging to a pH that would mess up your proteins. You'd have a pretty bad time trying to function on that kind of wild swing. Hemoglobin also won't let go of the oxygen it's carrying until it hits enough of this stuff in the first place. So you've got the oxygen delivery system keyed off the very thing your cells are throwing away. The kidneys then use it to help manage acid in the long run.

You're not actually feeding the cells with it. They just end up making it as a result of getting their energy. It is the plumbing and chemistry that happens after that which makes the stuff useful to the rest of the system.

It's mostly a matter of keeping your blood from getting too alkaline. You end up with a lot of acid from normal metabolic activities, and the only thing that can absorb it in any real quantity is bicarbonate. That bicarbonate has to be made from CO2 in the first place. If you got rid of all of the gas the way you might with hyperventilation, your pH would shoot up and your enzymes would stop working right. The hands going numb in that situation is the calcium in your blood getting yanked out of solution. The kidneys are also constantly leaning on that same pool to get rid of the acids you make.

You do pick up a little by swallowing the stuff in seltzer. That's just a small top off for a system that is almost entirely dependent on your own exhaling to get by.

CO2 is a waste product of cellular respiration. But it does have some real, non-obvious functions. Let me think through what those are.

The main one is that it drives the chloride shift in red blood cells. You swap out bicarbonate for chloride across the cell membrane, and that whole mechanism keeps the blood from becoming too acidic. Without that, you'd have severe acidosis. The bicarbonate buffer system is the dominant pH regulator in blood and it's built around CO2.

There's also the role in the cerebral vasculature. CO2 levels are the primary short term regulator of blood flow to the brain. Too little of it and vessels constrict too much. You see this in hyperventilation, where you blow off too much CO2 and end up lightheaded.

So the honest answer is that the body needs to get rid of it, but the mechanisms for getting rid of it happen to be doing a lot of other necessary work. You can't just eliminate the pathways without losing those other functions.

groups.question: If it's illegal to not have auto-insurance, why doesn't the government control and regulate auto-insurance as a Tax, rather than letting private companies sell you a mandatory service?
texts:
You've got the first part a little wrong. A few states let you get by with a posted bond or a demonstration that you've got the cash to cover a judgment. No one is universally forced to buy a policy from a private outfit. You can't drive without some sort of financial backstop in most places, but the backstop doesn't have to take the form of a premium.

You get your answer on the second part if you look at the track record of government run insurance in other fields. The moral hazard pretty much takes care of itself, people just don't get the same jolt from a public bill as they do from a private one. Then you end up with an overhead that no one was looking for. The final result is usually a service that is a lot slower than the private version and wound up costing more in the end. You are not going to avoid the bill by changing who writes it.

You're kind of mixing up two different things. The law makes you carry some kind of coverage, sure, but you get to pick out the company that provides it. That's a long way from a tax, which is you writing a check to the state and getting no direct return. The insurance contract is between you and a private firm that'll fork out money if you end up in a wreck.

You could get the same thing from a state run monopoly and a bunch of other countries do. That keeps you from paying out of pocket for a crash. But it doesn't get you out of having to sort out the problem of pricing risk. The government would end up slapping a flat rate on everyone since it has no way to figure out who the bad risks are. The private companies at least have a reason to try and work that out. You'd still get the rest of the same headaches, you'd just be getting them from a more complicated setup.

You get a cleaner price out of a bunch of competing companies than you would out of a single state fund. That's the only real advantage the private system has. If the state ran the thing you'd have one huge pool where your safe driving ends up bailing out everyone else's mistakes. You'd still pay your share of that loss but you wouldn't get any discount for it. A few countries actually do it your way and they do end up with the universal coverage you are apparently looking for. The price they get in return is a whole lot less competition.

That said the whole thing is pretty much a shakedown either way. The only difference is whether the people collecting the cut are the men in charge of the state or a set of stockholders. You are going to pay your share one way or the other to make up for the people who run off and leave the mess for somebody else to clean up.

You've actually got a few live experiments to look at. A handful of states have set up state run plans that act as a backstop, and a few have gone all in on a monopoly model. None of them have been able to shake out the problem of local risk. You've got a whole lot of different driving conditions to price out and the private actuaries are pretty good at that granular sort of thing. A single set of government rates would end up either screwing over the safe drivers in the bad areas or leaving a mess of holes in the coverage.

Then you have to stack on top of that the whole mess of getting a bunch of different localities to agree on a single pricing structure. You end up with a lot of political wrangling that the current arrangement of private competition mostly lets you sidestep. You get the monster of universal coverage without ever having to get all those different interests to agree on what it should cost.

You'd end up with the government doing all the actuarial math for thousands of different risk profiles. It's a hell of a lot more work than just taking a check and calling it done. You get to keep all the legal wrangling and claims handling in house too. You've seen what that looks like in health care, where the result was a bureaucracy so dense it got in the way of the thing it was supposed to provide. Some countries have tried this with auto coverage and got a little way down that road but never quite got to a clean solution.

That said the private arrangement has its own set of pretty nasty problems. You end up getting short changed by companies that write in a bunch of exclusions or game the system to pay out as little as possible. That gets in the way of the whole point of the requirement in the first place. Most places end up throwing in a state run option to keep the private ones from getting too cheeky. That doesn't get you to the neat simplicity of just making it a tax but it does put a bit of a lid on the worst of it.

It's mostly a math problem. The chance that you'll get in a smash is so different from person to person that a flat rate would have to be a pretty bad guess for almost everyone. You'd end up with a whole little tax code full of exceptions to get anywhere near fair. The private system gets that sorting done for you, in a clumsy way, through the price they quote you. You're also shifting the financial risk of a bad year off the general taxpayer and onto the company that sold you the policy. That contains a lot of the damage if things go south.

You're not entirely wrong that the whole thing is a bit ridiculous either. You are being forced to buy something you might not want from a group of people who are obviously in it for the profit. A few countries have tried to get around that by running the whole thing as a state scheme with a bunch of sliding scales to keep it from being too lopsided. It works, sort of, but it ends up trying to recreate the price sorting that the private companies do anyway.

It's mostly a matter of what you want to say to the voters. You can get the very same result by just slapping a tax on every driver and using that pool to pay for accidents. You'd get rid of all the forms and exclusions and the haggling that comes with a private sale. The only thing you'd lose is the appearance of a free market, and that appearance seems to be worth quite a bit to the people in charge. You also get to keep the real cost out of the open view of the people paying it. That sort of thing happened back when health care was left to the same sort of private arrangement.

It does cost you more in the end too. You end up shelling out a good chunk of that money for the overhead and profit margins that a state run version would probably get around.None of that prevents you from using the private companies to get the job done. You just have to make it so that you can't get along without them.

It mostly comes down to how you'd price it. You risk is a function of a dozen very specific things, the car you drive, your record, the neighborhood you live in, and so on. You can't get that level of discrimination out of a flat tax. You end up with the careful drivers paying to cover the sloppy ones and the sloppy ones getting a pretty good deal for it. That also kills off the main incentive to drive more carefully, since the price you pay isn't tied to what you actually do. If you wreck your car the tax you pay the next year isn't going to go up. You'd have to build in a whole separate penalty system to get any of that back.

You also run into the problem of just getting the rate right. Private companies have to cover their own losses or they go under, which gives them a pretty strong incentive to get their estimates right. You don't get that sort of feedback working through a tax. You do see a few states run their own plans, but that is almost always limited to the small group of people the rest of the market has turned away. Making the whole thing run that way gets run into all of the usual government service complaints you already have.

groups.question: if a human embryo isn't viable, by what mechanism does the body decide to terminate? What is it that goes "this isn't working, scrap it"?
texts:
There is no committee sitting around to make that call. What you are seeing is mostly the collapse of a positive feedback loop. A normal early pregnancy depends on the embryo putting out a decent amount of hCG. That hormone keeps the corpus luteum in the ovary cranking out progesterone, which in turn keeps the uterine lining intact. Skip the first step and the rest of the chain just falls apart. The lining sloughs off and the whole thing gets expelled. You have built in a fail safe that requires continuous proof the thing is working.

You get somewhat different machinery if the problem is immune in character. The placenta normally does a fair amount of work to keep the mother's defenses from going after it. If that concealment breaks down the maternal immune system will attack the thing as foreign. That attack does the rest of the work.

In the case of something like a molar pregnancy the signals get so badly scrambled that the body responds by rejecting the whole arrangement. Same general principle though. The pregnancy simply cannot supply the chemical proof needed to keep the machinery running.

There isn't a referee in there making a call. It's mostly the embryo failing to keep the whole thing propped up. Once the thing that's supposed to get implanted has to send out hCG to keep your own corpus luteum from falling apart. That luteum is the main source of the progesterone the lining needs. Miss that signal and the luteum starts to wither, the hormone level drops, and the lining just sloughs off in a way you'd recognize as a period. A lot of the time the whole arrangement just collapses from the inside out because the thing it was supposed to support was already a dud.

You do get some active contribution from the tissue the lining itself makes. Damaged cells in the area start putting off tissue factor which kicks the local blood clotting machinery into gear. That's the same sort of process that ends a normal cycle, it's just being coaxed along by the failure on the other end. So the "scrap" decision you're picturing is really just the default state of your own system getting to move forward.

There isn't really a referee out there making a call. You're mostly looking at a bunch of processes that have to keep getting the right signals to keep going. The embryo has to get the lining of the uterus to keep making progesterone. If it can't do that, the corpus luteum just runs out of steam and the whole thing sloughs off. You end up with the same result whether the problem is a bad set of chromosomes or a failed implantation. The body isn't so much evaluating the situation as it is failing to get the inputs it needs to carry on.

That said there are a few hard checkpoints. A lot of the chromosomal errors people think of as being found really just result in the thing stopping development on its own. The response you see is the maternal side of things simply giving up and resuming its normal cycle. It gets to look pretty a lot like some sort of conscious decision when you step back and look at the end result.

You mostly get a bunch of failures that end up looking like a decision. Most of the time it's just the implantation site being no good. The outer cells of the thing you're calling an embryo can't get a hold on your uterine wall the way they need to. No hold means no blood supply, and no blood supply means the whole arrangement winds down. That's probably the bulk of it. You don't need some sort of watchdog to notice the thing is a dud.

You do get a bit more in the way of active interference later on. Your immune system will sometimes take it upon itself to attack the thing, though nobody has a very good handle on what sets that off. And then there's the whole business of the original cell division going wrong and leaving you with a set of instructions that can't be carried out. In that case the thing simply runs out of instructions to keep going.

So you've got a collection of systems that are pretty bad at covering for each other. They end up with the same sort of result that a fairly smart overseer might have gotten to.

There's no little committee sitting around going "well, this one's a dud, let's nix it. You've mostly got a few different things all failing at the same time.

The big one is that the embryo simply can't get past its next developmental checkpoint, usually because of some chromosomal mix up. You've got something like 50 to 60 percent of conceptions that hit that wall. The thing just stops. At the same time the endometrium isn't on some multi month lock in. It's working on a very short window and if the right chemical handshakes don't happen it just sloughs off. You end up with what is in effect a very heavy period.

Once you get to the point of an actual implantation the embryo is supposed to start pumping out hcg. That's what keeps the corpus luteum from withering. It keeps the progesterone up. A nonviable thing won't make enough of that. The corpus luteum dies off, the progesterone falls, and the whole arrangement falls apart. So the closest you get to the body saying scrap it is just that the thing needed to keep it going never got there.

You'll occasionally see immune related rejection, but that's the exception rather than the rule. The overwhelming share of early losses are just the thing being unable to carry on.

It's mostly the absence of a "keep going" signal rather than some supervising mechanism hitting the kill switch. The whole thing runs on a positive feedback loop. The trophoblast cells that will become the placenta pump out hCG, and that hCG keeps your corpus luteum from winding down. The corpus luteum in turn keeps making the progesterone the uterine lining needs to hold together. If the embryo is a mess, it doesn't make enough hCG. The corpus luteum then does what it was going to do on schedule around two weeks out, it stops. The progesterone falls, the lining sheds, you're done. That accounts for the great bulk of early losses.

You also get some active opposition from the maternal side. The decidual NK cells that normally get stood down by a healthy implantation will attack one that isn't putting out the right immunosuppressive molecules. That's closer to an "scrap it" response, but it's really just the immune system failing to be overridden.

And the stuff that goes wrong in the first place is almost always chromosomal. The cells can't get very far, they stop making the signaling molecules the feedback loop needs, and the whole arrangement simply falls apart. You'd be looking for a decision where there just isn't one. It's more like a watch that won't wind.

There isn't really an arbiter sitting there taking a look and passing a sentence. It's closer to the whole thing just falling apart for lack of the one signal that was propping it up. The embryo is supposed to start pumping out hCG right around the time your next period would be due. That hCG is what keeps the corpus luteum from degenerating, and the corpus luteum is what's making the progesterone that keeps the uterine lining from shedding. Miss that hCG and the corpus luteum just wears out on its own. Progesterone drops, the lining breaks down, and you get a period that happens to include the failed conception. In very early cases the resorption is so complete you don't even notice it. The "default" state of the system is to menstruate. Pregnancy is the thing that has to be actively sustained, and when the sustaining signal fails the default takes over.

You do get some immune system involvement, particularly where tissue is quite abnormal, but that's more of a secondary effect than the primary driver. The main event is just the hormonal support running out.

There isn't some central committee that looks at the situation and votes to end it. Most of what you're seeing is just a chain of dependencies falling apart. The big one is HCG, the hormone the developing placenta is supposed to pump out. That hormone is what keeps your corpus luteum from withering, and the corpus luteum is what keeps the uterine lining in place. So if the embryo is chromosomally messed up it never gets to the point of making enough HCG. The hormone levels drop off, the lining breaks down, and the whole thing gets shed. You've got a miscarriage but nobody actually issued an order for it.

You'll also get mechanical versions of the same thing. The outside cells of the embryo might simply fail to get a firm toehold in the wall of the uterus, or they might not be able to tap into the local blood supply. Once that happens the thing just runs out of what it needs to keep going.

There's an immune piece to it too. The uterus normally keeps the local immune response pretty quiet so it doesn't attack the implanting embryo. If that balance gets thrown off the normal defenses end up doing in the pregnancy. That part is still pretty poorly understood though.

So the whole thing is less a decision than a set of things that only keep going as long as the previous step keeps feeding them.

The corpus luteum then does what it was going to do on schedule around two weeks out, it stops. The progesterone falls, the lining sheds, you're done. That accounts for the great bulk of early losses.

You also get some active opposition from the maternal side. The decidual NK cells that normally get stood down by a healthy implantation will attack one that isn't putting out the right immunosuppressive molecules. That's closer to an "scrap it" response, but it's really just the immune system failing to be overridden.

And the stuff that goes wrong in the first place is almost always chromosomal. The cells can't get very far, they stop making the signaling molecules the feedback loop needs, and the whole arrangement simply falls apart. You'd be looking for a decision where there just isn't one. It's more like a watch that won't wind.

The hormones that maintain the pregnancy (mainly hCG from the embryo, which keeps the corpus luteum pumping out progesterone) just stop. Without that signal, the endometrium sloughs off.

- If the embryo is developmentally failing, it doesn't produce enough hCG.
- The corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone and estrogen fall off.

groups.question: Why do tickets dispensed by arcade machines always seem to arrange themselves into neat piles?
texts:
It's mostly an illusion your brain builds out of a pretty rigid mechanical process. The spring that feeds the stack pushes out one ticket at a time, and the exit slot only lets a single card through. Since they are all cut to the exact same dimensions, gravity keeps them aligned along the long edge. You end up with that shingled effect that you see on a roof. It is the same principle as dealing out a deck of cards one at a time. Nobody stacked them, you are just watching the results of that one at a time delivery.

You would probably see the fall in a jam or if that spring got out of adjust. The tickets would start to fan out or get stuck and the whole thing would look a lot less orderly. You are definitely seeing a result of that mechanical regularity and your own habit of looking for a pattern in it.

You haven't really got any sorting going on. The tickets go in as a stack and they come out in the same order. You're peeling a few off the top and setting them down, and the next few land right on top of those. It's the same as pulling sticky notes off a pad. The little tray in front just stops the whole thing from sliding off a table. You'd get the same result if you pulled the entire stack out by hand and set it down.

You do end up with a mess if two get stuck together and then separate at a bad angle, or if the pusher gets a little out of line. That's the only time you'll see a single one off at a skew. The rest of the time you're just watching a orderly stack get a little shorter.

You probably get the effect more out of ticket machines than, say, a card deck, because the things coming out are so thin and uniform. You wouldn't notice the same thing with something more chunky or irregular to begin with.

It's mostly the screw inside the machine. They use a tight pitch auger to push one ticket out at a time through a little slot. That slot is your only exit point, so every ticket gets dropped from more or less the same spot. They have almost no sideways velocity, they're all the same size, and the stock is stiff enough not to splay. They just keep landing on the middle of the pile that's already there. You'd get the same thing if you dropped a stack of playing cards from the same point. The only reason they look so magical is that your eye latches onto the tidy result and skips over the odd one that lands askew.

You'll see the effect fall apart pretty fast if you get the machine to run for a long time. The pile eventually gets too tall, the top tickets start to fan out, and you end up with that lopsided thing you have to fish your winnings out of.

It's mostly the shape of the slot they have to get through. There's a fixed lip near the end that every single ticket has to clear, and that lip acts like a comb. You end up with each new one lined up exactly behind the last. It works the same way if you push a handful of playing cards through a narrow enough channel. The constraint gets applied to them in the same fashion over and over.

You only see a mess if a couple of the things get jammed up. At that point the result of them getting free depends on some pretty random detail. That is the only time the whole deal breaks down. You see the same principle at work in an index machine, or in a machine that feeds pages through a hole punch. Neither of those is doing anything magical to keep things straight.

They're cut out of a continuous roll so every one is the same size and shape. The machine then uses a little spring loaded plunger to push the top one forward. That plunger is held in a guide, so each ticket comes out at the same angle and the same spot. They then land on a small lip or tray that stops them from sliding off. You end up with a pile the way you get a stack of bills out of a purser. Same idea, just with worse paper.

You'd get a lot more mess if the tickets were even a little irregular, or if the dispensing mechanism let them come out at varying angles. The neatness is almost entirely an accident of how cheap and crude the whole mechanism is. It does only one thing, and it does it the same way every time.

It's mostly the slot they come out of. That narrow opening only lets a ticket through if it's more or less vertical, so you get a stream of them all facing the same way. Drop a bunch of identical playing cards through a keyhole and you get the same result. Once they hit the tray the next one just lands on top and the slight static and friction keeps it there. You're also probably ignoring the times one gets wedged or bounces off at an angle. You remember the tidy stack and forget the mess.

You'd get a pretty similar effect from a bunch of identical envelopes fed out of a sorting machine. It's not that the tickets have some inborn sense of order so much as that the whole setup strips out every arrangement but one.

It's the two rollers the ticket gets fed through. They run at slightly different speeds so the strip gets wound up on the way out. You get the same curl every single time since it's just set by the roller sizes. That's the same trick a printing press uses to get a page to curl back into a book.

You end up with a stack rather than a mess because the next ticket slides right on top of the last one. Every strip is trying to roll the same way so they keep piling up in that one direction. You'll get the same effect from those rolls of implementation paper you get at the pharmacy. They wouldn't end up so tidy if some of them were wound the other way.

You can get a pretty good look at the whole thing if you take the machine apart. You'll find the two rollers up top and a bit of rubber to get a grip on the stuff. It is such a simple piece of engineering to get so much order out of a bunch of junk.

You're mostly getting it from the machine. The tickets come out as one long strip with little score lines between them, and the tear off slot is just a fixed width. It acts like a die, snapping the strip at each score line so you get a rectangle of the same size every time. Dump a bunch of those identically shaped bits in the same spot and you've got a pile that looks pretty orderly. It's the same trick a perforated notepad uses to get you neat sheets. You do get a bit of help from the fact they're all the same, but the machine is doing all the real work of sorting.

You'd get a much messier result from something that let the bits out in random shapes or orientations. Try getting that same neatness from a bag of torn up confetti and you'll see the whole thing falls apart.

groups.question: How can you "feel" someone behind or near you?
texts:
You are getting a fair amount of information without looking. Your ears can put a sound somewhere in space by comparing the time and loudness that hits each one. A footstep or a breath is enough for that to work. Your eyes are also way more sensitive to movement on the far edges of your vision than they are to detail. A shape in that blurry zone will set off an alert. You will also notice a small change in the temperature on your skin from a body nearby. Your brain latches onto all of that and pieces it together pretty fast.

That last bit is usually what gets written up as some kind of mysterious sense. You have been acting in a way that would normally get you a response. Getting none of that is your brain filling in for an unseen cause. In the vast majority of cases that guess is wrong since there never was a person there.

Most of it is your ears doing their job. They pick up the soft shuffling of feet or the rustle of clothing way before your conscious mind sorts out what they are. Your brain then rushes in to fill in the blanks and it almost always fills them in with the idea of a person. You've also gotten pretty good at noticing the tiny changes in air a nearby body creates. That part is just you having spent a long time in an environment where mistaking a harmless sound for a predator was far less dangerous than missing a real one.

You can see the whole mechanism pretty clearly if you try it out. Get into a quiet room, close your eyes, and have a friend sneak up on you. You'll probably jump at the first bit of displaced air you notice. The jump happens first and the idea of the person almost always gets attached to it afterward. You have no way to sort out which one came first since the two are so tightly bound together.

You are mostly getting it from your eyes. The outer parts of your retina are stuffed with light sensitive rods that are way better at catching movement than the color sensitive ones in the middle. A faint shift in that region gets caught and your brain instantly fills in the rest. You then walk around convinced you saw a person. Your ears help out too since you can get a pretty good fix on the left and right of a sound. A footstep or a rustle gets locked into a position that your brain interprets as being directly behind you.

A fair amount of it is just your brain guessing. You have a model of the world you have built up from past experience and if that model says someone is likely to be there you will take the faintest hint and promote it to a definite sighting. It is a pretty efficient way to get along, you just have to put up with the occasional error.

Most of it is the hairs on the back of your neck. They've got little muscle fibers that make them stand up when some tiny air current or static charge hits them, and your brain has learned to read that as somebody is there. You get a fair bit of the same sort of information from your skin in general and from very faint sounds your attention isn't focused on. Your brain then takes all that half information and fills in a startlingly complete picture. It's doing that gap filling so fast and so confidently that it feels like you actually have a sixth sense. You almost certainly don't.

You'll notice the effect is a lot worse in the dark, which is a pretty good hint that you are working from a lot less raw data than you think. In the dark your brain has to reach further for that picture, and the result is a lot more likely to be wrong. That's why you'll sometimes get a full and very definite feeling of somebody standing right behind you when quite clearly no one is.

Your ears are doing most of the work. They pick up the faint creak of a floorboard or the rustle of clothing that your conscious mind hasn't sorted out yet. The brain then takes that raw data and slaps a "someone is there" label on it. You are also constantly scanning your peripheral vision for any movement, and a shadow there is enough to set your nerves on edge. That sudden bristling of the hair on your neck is just your startle response to some one of those small cues.

You are also primed to expect the worst. We are so used to the idea that people are watching us that we will read that suspicion into any number of otherwise unexplained sensations. Try the same thing in a situation where you had no reason to expect to be observed and you'll find the whole thing goes away. There isn't really any unknown faculty at work here.

You're mostly just running on a bunch of low grade signals your brain stitches together. You've got a pretty well drilled in habit of catching the faintest rustle of clothing or a slight change in the air. Sound bounces off a person's body in ways that change the whole picture too. Then your own sense of self preservation gets in there and jumps to the worst conclusion. All of that gets sorted out in your head so fast that the finished conclusion feels like some sort of real intuition. It would be worse off in the dark though. You'd be going almost entirely on your sense of smell. You can't consciously make out very many of the odors that carry that kind of information. They get handled on some pretty deep level by the part of your brain that manages your worst fears.

You are mostly getting it from your peripheral vision. Your eyes have a whole bunch of rods out in the side that are great at spotting a big change in the light but terrible at telling you what that change is. Your brain fills in the rest, and it pretty much always fills it in with something dangerous. At the same time your ears are picking up on the specific way a sound comes in from one side. The whole thing gets mixed up in your head and it ends up looking a lot like you actually know something is there.

groups.question: How do owners of non-profit organizations or people who are "experts" in really odd things make money? Are most of them just retired or do they get paid by someone to do these things?
texts:
You're mostly getting paid by the people who sign the checks for the work. The non-profit label doesn't mean the people running it work for free. It just means the left over cash can't get distributed to owners. You've got a salary that comes out of the pot that donations and grants fill up. The whole game is basically writing grant proposals to foundations and government agencies. You describe your program in a lot of fancy language, and if it checks enough boxes they write you a check. That check covers your salary along with the actual work. Big enough organizations also build up an endowment, which is just a pile of invested money whose interest keeps you running. You see that a lot with university based operations.

The weird specialist angle is a little different. You've got a professor at some college getting a modest base salary, then stacking on top of it a bunch of small grants to keep studying their particular beetle. They'll also pick up a bit here and there from writing a book or giving talks. None of that usually adds up to a lot of cash, which is part of why you do see a fair number of people in the situation you're describing. They've got some retirement savings or family money that lets them get away with it. You get a decent mix of all these things rather than any one of them.

It's mostly a patchwork. You've got the endowment model where some long dead rich person left some money to invest, and the returns pay the bills. That gets you pretty far without needing a patron. Then you have the grant writing game which is honestly a full time job in itself. Plenty of these people are doing that between projects. The expert angle also opens up book deals and speaking fees which will pay for quite a bit of research. You do hit on the occasional rich backer but that is the exception that ends up in the press.

You are probably mostly looking at people who have managed to string a few of these together. None of them alone would hold the thing up. It is the combination that keeps the more out there pursuits from just falling over. The small salary the organization pays the person in charge is usually a lot less than what the same work would bring in elsewhere. You have to be pretty set on the subject to accept that.

It's a lot more like a regular job than you'd think. You'll find plenty of people doing this as their main line of work, they just take a pay cut in exchange for the subject matter. The whole thing gets kept afloat by a patchwork of foundation grants, membership dues, and the occasional endowment. You spend a ton of time writing out those grant proposals, which is why you so often see the actual experts kept pretty far away from the money getting end. You've got your share of retirees and voluntters too, and at the very small end of the spectrum that might be the whole picture.

Once the operation gets to be of any size you end up looking a lot like a business with a different source of revenue. The pay is a little lighter, the paperwork a lot heavier, and that's about as far as the romance of the thing goes.

You're mostly getting a regular salary, you just get it out of a bunch of different places. A non profit can't hand profits out to the people running it, but it can pay them a wage. That wage has to be defensible, you can't just make up some wild number. The organization then goes and gets the money to cover that from grants, membership fees, ticket sales to events, and the occasional big check from a rich person. You see the same thing with the weird subject matter experts, they'll pick up a little from an adjunct teaching gig here and there. Then they get a bit more by giving a talk or putting out a book to a small but very dedicated audience.

You will run into a fair number of people in these positions who are living off a pension or some inherited fortune. That is the part that the whole thing falls apart without, since none of the pay you can get from the field itself is going to be very much. So you've got a patchwork of all these little streams holding the thing up rather than any one reliable source of income.

You'll see all of it and then some. You get a scattering of the retired rich type, and they're mostly in astronomy or the natural sciences. That's where you end up seeing the private observatories or the personal collections of butterflies. But that's really the exception. The people you are more likely to run into are getting out a university sabbatical or a small research grant. That grant stuff is a little different from a regular salary since you are only paid to get a specific set of results. You also get a lot of it from the interest on a big endowment that some benefactor has left behind. That last one looks a lot like retirement from the outside but it is a very specific sort of funding.

You are not going to get a clean answer here because the whole thing is a patchwork. The person you are looking at is almost certainly putting together some combination of these to keep things going. You might even find that a person moves from one of these modes to another from year to year.

You usually get both in the same deal, just with a few extra links in the chain. The guy who wants to preserve an obscure 19th century typeface isn't going to pay for it himself. He gets a small grant from a foundation. You look up that foundation and it turns out a bunch of dead moneylenders set it up with instructions to do exactly this sort of thing. So the original source of the cash is very often a retired or deceased person, but they arent running the project. The expert in the obscure thing is almost never getting paid by the project itself. You get some small honorarium for giving a lecture that happens to further the project, and you get the rest from some other source.

The whole scheme only works as long as you keep the thing small. The moment you try to get it to scale you run out of people willing to underwrite it on principle. You can't get big corporations to get behind the preservation of some vanishing dialect, and the people who will do it only have so much to spread around. You end up with a lot of little things that wouldnt exist for a minute if you tried to make them pay their own way.

It's mostly a patchwork. You'll see a lot of foundation money going to these places, since a bunch of rich people get off on underwriting things that are too small for the government to bother with. Endowments are another big一根, some dead person usually left a fortune to keep the whole thing going. You do get a fair number of retirees filling in on a voluntary basis, but that doesn't get you very far on its own. A lot of the folks you see also pick up extra work on the side, maybe writing a book or doing some consulting. That outside money is what keeps the lights on when the grants run out.

You probably won't find any single one of those sources that does the whole job. The whole setup only works because you've got all of them more or less at the same time.

It's mostly a mix, and the mix differs a bunch. Non-profits run on a pile of small grants from foundations, some government money, and individual donations. On top of that they charge for the thing they do. A non-profit health clinic charges (reduced) fees, a non-profit school charges tuition. The people running them draw a salary out of that, the board just keeps the salaries from getting out of line. You aren't seeing any of that if you're only looking at the "non-profit" label.

The weird-expert crowd is more of a grab bag. A government agency will pay you to go find out things they need to know. A foundation will write out a grant if your weird subject happens to be their thing. You can get a book deal or a pile of paid lecture gigs. And yeah, a fair number of them are just independently wealthy and doing it as a hobby. You'd be hard pressed to tell from the outside which is which. The oddness of the subject doesn't really change the mechanics any.

You probably just aren't seeing the money changing hands, since none of it looks like a regular job.

But it's not the dominant model. Most of the people you'd see giving talks or writing up their findings are getting some form of institutional support. That grant stuff is a little different from a regular salary since you are only paid to get a specific set of results. You also get a lot of it from the interest on a big endowment that some benefactor has left behind. That last one looks a lot like retirement from the outside but it is a very specific sort of funding.

You are not going to get a clean answer here because the whole thing is a patchwork. The person you are looking at is almost certainly putting together some combination of these to keep things going. You might even find that a person moves from one of these modes to another from year to year.

You usually get both in the same deal, just with a few extra links in the chain. The guy who wants to preserve an obscure 19th century typeface isn't going to pay for it himself. He gets a small grant from a foundation. You look up that foundation and it turns out a bunch of dead moneylenders set it up with instructions to do exactly this sort of thing. So the original source of the cash is very often a retired or deceased person, but they arent running the project. The expert in the obscure thing is almost never getting paid by the project itself. You get some small honorarium for giving a lecture that happens to further the project, and you get the rest from some other source.

The whole scheme only works as long as you keep the thing small. The moment you try to get it to scale you run out of people willing to underwrite it on principle. You can't get big corporations to get behind the preservation of some vanishing dialect, and the people who will do it only have so much to spread around. You end up with a lot of little things that wouldnt exist for a minute if you tried to make them pay their own way.

It's mostly a mix, and the mix differs a bunch. Non-profits run on a pile of small grants from foundations, some government money, and individual donations. On top of that they charge for the thing they do. A non-profit health clinic charges (reduced) fees, a non-profit school charges tuition. The people running them draw a salary out of that, the board just keeps the salaries from getting out of line. You aren't seeing any of that if you're only looking at the "non-profit" label.

The weird-expert crowd is more of a grab bag. A government agency will pay you to go find out things they need to know. A foundation will write out a grant if your weird subject happens to be their thing. You can get a book deal or a pile of paid lecture gigs. And yeah, a fair number of them are just independently wealthy and doing it as a hobby. You'd be hard pressed to tell from the outside which is which. The oddness of the subject doesn't really change the mechanics any.

You probably just aren't seeing the money changing hands, since none of it looks like a regular job.

groups.question: If residential solar is such a good investment, how come 95% percent of homes don't have it yet?
texts:
You could ask that about almost anything. If buying a house is such a good deal, why do so many people keep renting? You get the same 95 percent number from people who just can't come up with the 30 or 40 grand in front. That's the whole story in most cases. You need a loan and you need to expect to be in that house long enough to get the payback. A bunch of people simply don't fit that. You're not seeing a verdict on whether the thing is a good bet, you're seeing a verdict on who has the cash flow to take it on.

That said it isn't a uniformly good bet either. The math changes pretty fast depending on local electricity prices and how much sun you get. You might do the whole exercise and find out you won't come out ahead for a very long time.

It's mostly a cash problem. You can make the math work out over twenty five years, but almost nobody has that kind of money to throw down at the front end. A huge slice of the country is also stuck in rental situations where the person footing the bill never gets to see the payoff. On top of that the local red tape is a real drag. You end up waiting months for permits and a spot on the utility's connection list. You do start to see the numbers move once a state steps in to paper over a few of those snags.

You will probably keep seeing the same gap until those barriers get smoothed out some more though. The underlying deal is there it just isn't in a shape that most folks can get to.

You've got the numbers pretty far off. You are looking at a market where maybe two to three out of every hundred homes have the setup. That missing big chunk is mostly made up of people who rent. They have no say in what goes on the roof. Then you get the owners in places where the local utility doesn't offer good enough offsets to make the math work. And a whole lot of people just can't come up with the cash up front even if they can see the long term payoff. The whole thing is so heavily dependent on your particular county and neighborhood that it is hard to call it a sure thing.

You are also getting stuck on the red tape side of things. Tons of the older style housing developments still have covenants that effectively keep the panels from going up. And the business of getting the power company to come out, do their inspections, and get hooked in has a way of eating up a lot of the time the thing would have been making money.

You're mostly looking at the wrong group. The people who put panels on the roof are almost always in a situation that the rest of the country isn't. They've got the cash to front the cost, they plan to live there long enough to see it paid off, and they can get some pretty aggressive state tax breaks. That last bit is a big one since it can be the only thing that makes the math work. On top of that you run into a real mess of local zoning laws and the fact that a lot of old houses have electrical systems that would need to be ripped out.

The math also just stops working in a bunch of places where the local utility has kept rates fairly low. If you aren't paying much for the power you get from the grid the alternative starts to look a lot less attractive. So you end up with a situation where the investment is fantastic for a select few and simply not on the table for the 95 percent who don't have that exact mix of advantages.

You run up against a whole lot of different things. The sticker price is the first, and for most people 20 or 30 grand is just out of reach. The federal tax credit scraps some of that, but you still have to have enough income to claim it and a tax bill to apply it against. You also have to be in the house long enough to outlive the payback period, which is out of the question for anyone renting. Add in a pretty bad installer marketplace full of pressure tactics, and a patchwork of local permitting rules, and it starts to feel like too much trouble. A fair chunk of it is just that people are out of the loop on what the system will actually do for their bills.

You get a very different picture in countries like Germany or Australia. Over there the utility rates and the political set up have made the whole thing far easier to get into. So the tech isn't secretly a bad bet. You are just getting caught up in a bunch of very real practical snags. The tax credit is also due to expire in a couple of years, and that has had the effect of making plenty of folks wait and see.

You're sorting by the wrong variable. Plenty of great deals go mostly untouched because the math only works out for a specific set of circumstances. You need a lot of unshaded southern exposure to make the numbers work. You also have to be around to use the power you make. And when you sell the house you can't take that unpaid for equipment with you. The utility you are hooked up with matters just as much. Some will cut you a check for the extra power you send their way and some won't. Change any of those local conditions and the whole thing stops being a good deal.

You see the same thing with index funds. It is a far better way to save for retirement than almost anything else. And the vast majority of people still sit on their money in savings accounts. The opportunity is there for sure but it only acts like one for the person who happens to be in the right situation to take it.

You've got the first part of that backwards. The numbers only work out for people who own their place and live there long enough to see the payoff. That rules out every renter in the country right off. Then you have to factor in the local utility rates and how much actual sun the roof gets. Some places get so little that the panels never pay for themselves. So you end up with a situation where the thing is a real winner for a subset of the population and a total loss for the rest. It's the same dynamic that keeps a lot of people from buying a car outright. The fact that they rent one doesn't prove the purchase would have been a mistake.

You'll also run into the problem that the whole thing is a huge chunk of cash to get started. A lot of people just can't get over that first wall. It has nothing to do with the final outcome for the people who do get past it.

You've got the percentages a little jumbled. It's more like four or five percent of US homes have panels, not the five percent you'd get from your 95 figure. And that small number is mostly a product of the local real estate market. You need a roof that gets a certain amount of unobstructed sun, which rules out a huge chunk of the country. Even for the people who do have the right roof that five or six figure sticker price is a tough pill to swallow. The federal tax credit makes a dent in it but it still leaves most folks out in the cold. Add in the fact that a bunch of utility companies are still fumbling with the rules for buying that power back and you get a pretty clear picture of the whole mess.

You end up with a product that is only financially workable for a fairly narrow class of people. It works out fine if your situation happens to fit that class but it ends up looking like a wildly inefficient use of capital for everyone else. That is mostly why the numbers are the way they are.

groups.question: Why don't any larger animals have compound/multiple eyes like bugs do?
texts:
It's mostly a math problem. Each little tube in a compound eye only gets you a few pixels of information. You'd need an absolutely ridiculous number of them to get the sharpness you'd want, and the brain to sort all that out would end up being huge. You get a wide picture out of it, sure, but the whole thing is sort of a mosaic. Fine for a wasp that mostly needs to sense something moving, useless for trying to make out a face. A single big lens with a bunch of refracting elements inside gets you much more out of the same amount of space.

It isn't impossible to get the arrangement to work on a big scale. Some of the squid and octopus out in the deep have pretty vast versions of it. You just end up with a night vision sort of sense that trades off a lot of the finer detail. The whole thing gets to be too unwieldy to be worth the trouble for most land animals.

It's mostly a math problem. You get a sharp picture out of a compound eye by jamming in a really large number of tiny lenses. That works for a gnat because the whole thing is so small. If you tried to build one for a horse you'd need a mind boggling number of those little units just to get a view you could do anything with. You'd also end up with a very fuzzy result because each individual unit has such a narrow field.

There is also the whole question of what on earth you would do with all that data. The brain would have to merge a vast number of separate low quality inputs. You just can't get the same sort of fine detail that way. That is why the single large lens with a clear fluid to focus through ended up being the more useful path. You do see a few animals that have muddled the two approaches to get around some of these limits. Most of the octopus family uses a version of that.

You mostly do. You've just got it in a different package. The deep sea giant isopod gets by with two separate optical systems in one eye, and the cuttlefish runs a sort of hybrid. You just aren't going to find the classic faceted design on anything as big as a horse. That design hits a resolution ceiling set by the size of the individual facets. You can't get around that, so you end up with a very wide but pretty fuzzy picture. A single big lens gets around that by throwing in a lot more light and focusing it much more tightly. That is pretty much what a big hunting animal needs. You give up the wide angle view to get the fine detail.

You might imagine some kind of crossover that gets you the best of both. It has actually been tried a few times in the way I mentioned. In the end the two main strategies for seeing just work out to be the best bet on opposite ends of the size scale.

groups.question: Why are there no Grape flavored Yogurts?
texts:
You can find 'em, you just won't see them stacked up at the front of the cooler. A few companies have tried it and mostly got the same depressing results. It turns out grape has a real headache of a headnote, something almost medicinal that yogurt just can't mellow out. You get strawberry or peach and the mild sourness of the dairy works with the fruit. Grape ends up making the whole thing taste like a cough drop. You end up with something that just isn't worth making in the first place.

That said the whole thing is really a problem of how they get the flavor. They are usually forced to rely on seed and skin extracts to get the effect they want. Those same extracts are what ruin the finish. If they could get a more rounded and less aggressive grape taste they might get somewhere. They just haven't been able to do that yet.

You can probably find some small operation that has tried it, but the big names all passed on it. The pectin that makes grapes so nice in a jelly makes a real mess in a milk mixture, you get a curdling that nobody can get to look right. Then you have the tannins to deal with, which give that sort of dry astringency that just fights with the smooth mouthfeel you are going for. You end up with something that tastes like grape juice has been sloshed over a regular plain variety.

On top of that the whole thing runs into the fact that people have a very specific idea of what grape should taste like. That idea comes from the candy and keeps them from accepting the real thing. Once the company that tried to get it off the ground saw the test keepers falling for neither, they had little reason to keep trying. You are actually more likely to find some sort of grape colored and grape candied fake than you are to find the real article.

There actually are a few, you just mostly run into them in Europe or in some supermarket house brands. You'll find them if you look. They're just way rarer than the strawberry or banana stuff, and that comes down to a couple of annoying practical things.

You need an awful lot of grape juice to get the flavor and the purple color through, and grape juice is so cloyingly sweet that it throws the whole thing off. You end up with something that tastes like candy on a dairy base. The tannins in the grapes are another headache, they give that slightly astringent, dry mouth feeling that just fights with the milk. Strawberry kind of melts into the yogurt in a way grape never manages. The result is a weird and one note flavor people seem to decide they don't want to keep around.

You'll get a similar story with other fruit, though grape seems to hit every one of these problems at once.

You're bump up against the fact that strawberry and vanilla are just way safer bets. Almost everybody likes those two and they work as a base for a bunch of other things. Grape is a lot more of a split thing. People either go for it or get weird about the color. That smaller and more scattered crowd isn't going to generate the same sales. You do see the stuff in the frozen section or in those little single serve cups. You just have to go look for it. The same is true for a lot of other fruits like peach or pear. You just notice the grape one more since you see that flavor on the cereal boxes all the time.

You might also be running into the fact that the actual fruit gets in the way of the color you have in your head. The fruit itself is going to turn a milk base into some kind of brownish purple. Getting that deep royal violet you are used to seeing on the packages of gummy bears requires a fairly heavy hand with the food dyes. That is something a lot of the bigger brands are pretty quick to steer clear of.

You can actually get it, it's just weirdly hard to find. The big national brands basically pass on it. Grape has a really strong one note punch that fights with the tartness of the milk. You end up with something that's either extra sharp or cloyingly sweet. That deep purple color also makes the end product look a bit unappetizing. And since kids make up the bulk of the fruit yogurt market, the companies just keep doubling down on the strawberry and banana those kids already have a handle on. You will have better luck looking at the store brand section of a Walmart or Target.

That said you are running into a pretty well established cycle. Something gets left off the big lists, which means fewer stores carry it, which in turn gives the companies even less reason to make it. It isn't that the thing is impossible, it is just that it never got the initial push to get out of that bind.

You can actually find a few, mostly in convenience stores or from some of the old Soviet style brands. They're just really uncommon. The trouble is that grape's flavor compounds react badly with the lactic acid in dairy. You end up with this sort of soapy, metallic edge that you don't get with strawberry or peach. You have to load in extra flavoring to get around that, which then makes the whole thing taste worse.

You've also got a bit of a training issue. Almost everyone has an idea of what grape is supposed to taste like from Jello and soda, and that particular flavor is very hard to reproduce in a milk base. A few companies tried to get there, got a batch of awful reviews, and just gave up. You see the same thing with grape in ice cream.

It's not that some law forbids the combination, it's just that the two things are pretty much at odds with each other.

You are probably just seeing what your local supermarket has chosen to stock. They have been around in the past and you will still find them in a few other markets. It comes down to the fact that the big companies keep churning out strawberry or peach. Those milder acids play off the milk base a lot more smoothly. Grape has that extremely distinctive and sometimes cloying sweetness which tends to get muddied out. You are not missing some long lost tradition you just ran into a business decision to stick to the sure things.

The same thing is happening with a lot of other fruits. You probably will not see a lot of blackberry or purple passionfruit either. That does not mean the recipe is impossible it only means the people in charge of the production lines decided it was not worth the risk.

You can get them, you just can't find them in a US grocery store. Dannon and Borden both made them a few decades back. What you're noticing is that the formula got dropped.

It comes down to the fact that grape works in Jell O and Kool Aid and gummy bears because those things are loads of sugar. The sugar drowns out grape's naturally sharp, almost vinegary back end. You put that same thing into a mellow dairy base and the weirdness sticks out. Cherry gets the same treatment. You can find cherry in a pudding and it seems fine, try it in yogurt and people get a little squirmy.

You try it out, it sells dramatically worse than the strawberry stuff, and you kill it off. That's the whole thing. Nobody is holding out on grape out of some deep food science principle, the first few trials just didn't work out. You'll get better luck in a few other countries where the whole thing isn't as dependent on that one safe fruit.

groups.question: What are the curving lines that appear in digital photos of computer screens?
texts:
You're seeing a moiré pattern. Both the screen and the camera have a super fine grid of elements, pixels on one side and photosites on the other. Those two grids will almost never line up perfectly, and the way they interfere with each other is what your eyes pick up as those moving bands. The rainbow coloring is just the same thing happening at slightly different angles for the red, green, and blue light. You can usually make it go away by changing your distance from the monitor or the angle at which you are shooting it. You see the same sort of thing when you look at a wire fence from far enough away that the bars start to blur into a pattern of their own.

You will get it much less if you use a camera with a very high resolution, since the finer grid of the sensor makes for a less obvious interference. Most of the older cameras you will find in phones are right in the range where the effect is pretty strong.

You are seeing a moire pattern. Both the screen and the camera lens have a regular grid of dots, the pixels. When you look at them through the other, those two grids superimpose. If the spacing is almost the same but not quite, your eye makes out a new, much larger pattern of light and dark bands. That is what the wavy lines are. Change the angle or the distance and the pattern will shift and change. You get the colored version of this because the interfering grids are sorting the red, green and blue subpixels out into separate bands. If you did the same thing with a black and white camera the lines would still be there, they'd just be in gray.

You are probably also catching a clash between the refresh rate of the monitor and the frame rate of the camera. That has nothing to do with the pixel grids and it makes the pattern roll up and down the picture. The two effects happen at the same time so you end up taking them in as a single thing.

That's a moire pattern. Both the screen and your camera sensor are made of very fine regular grids of dots, and when you photograph one with the other the two grids interfere. Your eyes then pick up the big slow moving bands that the two fine grids combine to make. It's the same effect you get if you hold two wire fences in front of each other at a slight angle.

You get the rainbow coloring because the screen's dots are actually little groups of red green and blue subpixels, and those groups line up and fail to line up with the camera's dots in a repeating way. The bands curve because the two grids rarely end up perfectly parallel to each other. You are almost always shooting from some perspective angle, and a bit of extra tilt gets added in. Nudge your position around and you will see the bands move, and at just the right geometry the two grids match up and the whole thing clears out.

You can get the same thing with an old TV, which is why you used to see it so much with the much coarser and more visible raster of those sets. Modern screens with their very fine subpixels make the effect harder to bring out, but it is still there.

It's a timing mismatch between the two machines. Your monitor repaints itself in horizontal bands from the top down, doing so sixty or one hundred and twenty times a second. The camera has its own idea of when to sample an image. When those two cycles aren't in step the snapshot catches the screen in the middle of a refresh. The top of the picture shows one state of the screen and the bottom shows an earlier one. That mismatch is what you see as a set of wavy bands.

They take on a rainbow cast because of the way the sub pixels are laid out. The red, green and blue elements line up in a very fine pattern and the interference spreads the colors out a bit. You get the same kind of thing if you try to photograph the pattern of a wire fence. Bump your camera's shutter speed around and the lines will move or sometimes clear up entirely. The usual name for the whole business is moire.

They're a moire pattern. Your phone's camera has a regular grid of pixels and the monitor you're pointing it at has its own regular grid. When you line up two of those grids that aren't perfectly matched you get an interference pattern, the same thing you'd see looking through one chain link fence at another. The fact that the lines curve has to do with the two grids being at slightly different angles to each other. The colored bands are the camera's red, green and blue color filters getting out of step with the monitor's red, green and blue subpixels.

You'll get the same thing looking at a close packed honeycomb through a wire screen. If you move the camera around the lines will change shape and they can even disappear and reappear at different places. You can't get rid of them entirely short of changing the angle or distance between the two grids.

It's a moiré pattern. Your camera has a grid of light sensors and the monitor has a grid of light emitting pixels. When you photograph one with the other those two grids end up slightly out of step. The mismatch between them creates a new, much larger pattern that your eye picks out as those wavy bands. It's the same effect you get when you look at the mesh of a ball park fence through another piece of netting.

You've probably seen the bands shift and change character if you move the camera a bit. That's the two grids getting in and out of alignment. You can sometimes get rid of the worst of it by changing your distance or angle of attack. You can't get rid of it entirely so long as you are sampling a grid with another grid. You'd have to let the camera take the picture through a lens that deliberately blurs the fine detail of the screen.

It's a moire pattern, same thing you get holding two wire fence sections at an angle. The camera sensor has its own fixed grid of light sensitive elements and that grid ends up at a slightly different scale than the one on the screen. Your brain sorts out the tiny dots into a smooth image, but the camera just faithfully records the two sets of lines. When they line up you get those slow moving waves. Move the camera in and out or tilt it and you'll see the whole thing change.

You are probably not thinking of the old vertical bars you used to see on tube televisions. That was a different problem where the rate at which the lights were being dimmed didn't match the rate the camera took its pictures. You still get something of the sort if the two rates are close but not exactly the same. It is just that the two grids are what get you in the situations you are describing.

You are looking at a beat frequency. Your camera has its own grid of light sensors and the screen has a grid of colored subpixels. When those two grids are almost but not quite the same size, their overlapping yields a much slower changing pattern the way you hear two nearly matching notes produce a slow pulsing. You get the wavy shapes because the two grids aren't exactly parallel. Twisting the camera a little changes that angle and makes the whole thing crawl. You get the same thing if you try to photograph a fine woven cloth.

It is a little different with the old style interlaced television. In that case you are also getting into trouble because the camera is trying to capture a picture that is actually being built up in two separate time steps.
