groups.question: Why did TV and computer screens used to flicker in videos, and now they don't?
texts:
It's mostly a story of how the picture got made. The old tubes painted the picture with a fast moving electron beam that hit phosphor dots on the glass. Those dots lit up and then very quickly faded to black, so the beam had to come back and paint the same spot over and over. Your eyes caught the little dips in brightness between each pass. That was the flicker. You got a little of it from the horizontal sweeps too, but the once a second vertical pass was the part you really noticed.

You got rid of the problem by changing the whole thing. Liquid crystal and light emitting diode screens just hold a given level of light until someone tells them to change it. There is no fading glow to get in the way. On top of that the industry kept pushing refresh rates up, so even the technologies that still work in a sweep are now sweeping too fast for your eyes to keep up with. You will still get a little of it out of some LED backlights that get pulsed to fake a lower brightness, but that is a different animal from the old thing.

You are mostly seeing a recording artifact rather than something the screen itself is doing. Old CRTs painted their picture by sweeping a beam from the top down and then starting over. The phosphors you were looking at were actually fading out between one sweep and the next, so the whole image pulsed at 50 or 60 times a second. When you filmed that with a movie camera that opened and closed its shutter 24 times a second you got a beat frequency. That is the fast rolling band you see on old home movies.

You got rid of it on both ends. Flat panel screens hold an image in place and get it replaced so many times a second that the eye stops seeing a pulse. At the same time digital cameras are easy to clock to the exact rate of the thing they are looking at. The two simply no longer get in each other's way.

You will still hit the old problem if you take your phone into a place with old style fluorescent lighting. Those tubes are doing the same sort of thing and your camera has to work out how to deal with them.

You've got it backwards a little. The screens weren't the problem, the light they were showing off was. You were looking at incandescent or fluorescent stuff that pulsated to match the local power line. In the US that was 120 times a second, in a lot of Europe it was 100. If you shot that with a camera that wasn't perfectly matched up to that pulse you got those rolling dark bands. You got the same thing if you took a 60 frame a second picture and played it back on a 50 frame a second set.

You got rid of it by changing the way you put the whole thing together. Once you started shooting in digital at 24, 25 or 30 frames a second and then pushing that to the screen with a fixed pulldown the two rates were locked together. The light source, the camera and the display all ended up in step. You'd still see the old毛病 if you stuck a mismatched camera in front of a 60 hertz light, you just don't run into it in the stuff that gets finished off.

It's mostly a scan method thing. The old tubes had to paint the whole picture with a single narrow beam of light. That beam zipped down the screen to draw one thin line at a time and then had to jump back to the top to start over. Your eyes kept seeing the dark gaps between all those lines. The beam had to redo the whole job a bunch of times every second to fool you into seeing a solid image, and that periodic redoing is what you took in as flicker. You could cut down on it by making the beam go around faster, say 100 or 120 times a second instead of 50 or 60. You still had the same gap problem though. The stuff you are looking at now got rid of it by lighting every single dot at the same time. The panels just hold that image until they are told to change it.

You will still run into a version of the old problem if you shoot one of the old tubes with a modern camera. The camera has its own sampling rate and that ends up in a weird conflict with the tube. That is what gives you those strange moving bands you see in the recording. Your own eyes would never have caught that.

You're mostly seeing two different clocks get in each other's way. Old CRTs drew the picture one horizontal scan line at a time, then went to the top and did it again 50 or 60 times a second. If you filmed that with a camera running at 24 or 30 frames a second the two rates wouldn't line up. You'd get a dark band that rolled down the picture, or the whole thing would get brighter and darker from frame to frame. You can still get that today if you shoot an old tube TV with the wrong camera settings.

The new flat panels got rid of the visible scan line entirely. They also tend to run at 120 hertz or more, which pushes that kind of interference out of the range a movie camera can catch. A lot of the cheaper ones still use a pulse width modulation to get different brightness levels, but they do it so many times a second that the camera just sees a steady image. You would probably still see it if you slowed the footage down a whole lot.

It's mostly the difference between how the two kinds of glass work. The old tube types painted the picture with a fast moving electron beam that left the screen dark for a split second between passes. You probably never saw those little dark gaps in normal use, but a movie camera running at 24 frames a second would catch just enough of them to make the whole thing dance. You've probably seen the cousin of that problem as those slow bands that roll up a projected image.

The flat panels you use now just keep the last picture fully lit until the next one is ready. There is no dark gap to get caught by a mismatched camera, so that particular trouble goes away. You'll still get the rolling band effect now and then, you just won't get the old fast shimmer. None of this has to do with the movies themselves, since the 24 frame rate hasn't actually changed.

It's mostly a matter of how the images got made. The old CRT sets, whether on a TV or a PC, worked by shooting a little beam of electrons across a screen of phosphor. That beam painted out the picture line by line and then had to start back at the top. It did the whole thing 50 or 60 times a second. The phosphor would light up as the beam hit it and then start to fade until the next pass. Your eye was just fast enough to catch that on and off cycle. You could see it pretty easily if you waved your hand in front of the set.

They kept pushing the refresh rate up to get the cycle too fast to see, but the real fix was ditching the whole beam thing. LCD, LED, and OLED panels have a complete grid of little elements that just stay lit. There's no sweeping beam, so there's no on and off for the phosphors to fade through. You can still get a little flicker from the way the backlight is pulsed, but they've mostly ironed that out.

It's mostly a matter of two things not being in step. The old tube screens you had to redraw the whole picture 50 or 60 times a second to get it to look continuous. That's fast enough that your own eyes will mostly ignore the interruptions. A video camera doesn't get that same benefit. It samples the picture at its own rate, and when that rate doesn't match up with the screen's you get a visible pulsing in the recording. You could sometimes see it with your own eyes too if you looked at the right angles.

You've since got around that in a couple of ways. You threw more refresh cycles at the problem, and you switched over to the flat panel types that don't have to paint their pictures in a sweeping beam. The recording side also got smarter about locking the camera to the screen it was shooting. You don't run into the mismatch so much anymore.

You may have noticed that the numbers were a little odd, 59 and 59.94 instead of a round 60. That was the old screens being built to run off of the AC power that was available, 60 cycles in this country and 50 in much of the rest of the world. That little historical detail is mostly of academic interest these days.

groups.question: A couple days ago, a 300 year old Stradivarius violin was stolen (and later found.) What would be the point of stealing something so famous that anyone who can afford the million-dollar price tag would recognize as a stolen item?
texts:
You're not trying to sell it to the open market. You'd never get that million dollar figure at auction with the thing on the FBI's stolen list. What you do is find one specific private collector who wants it badly enough to pretend not to know where it came from. The fame actually helps there, since you don't have to do any of the provenance work to prove it's a Strad. Anyone who knows the world of violins will know it in five seconds.

Then again, the most likely play is ransom. You've got something so obviously valuable and so obviously identifiable that the owner or the insurance company can't afford not to pay. They're going to pay a lot less than the full value, but they are going to pay. You could never get that same leverage with some nameless instrument no one would miss.

You could also strip away the varnish and knock off the identifying marks to break the chain of recognition. That's a lot of work, and it shaves real money off the asking price. So most of the time the thieves just let the instrument's notoriety do the work for them.

You'd only ever get a fraction of the real value for it. You might fence it to some local naive buyer who has no idea, or use the thing to hold the owners for a payoff. That last one is actually pretty common. You get it back and the insurers write a check. It works around the whole recognition problem because the people you're dealing with already know the score. You might also be in it for the ego or the thrill, which is easy to pull off when the whole ownership circle is small enough to name off the top of your head.

The quick recovery you are seeing isn't really that unusual either. The same tiny group of people who know what you've got are the people most motivated to push the police to get it back. You pretty much can't keep the thing for long.

You don't sell it to a museum or a concert hall. You sell it, in cash and through a long string of intermediaries, to some private person who is going to keep it in a closet. That person isn't going to publicly display the thing or register it with any authority. You're looking for a buyer who really wants to own a Strad and has no particular need to prove how he got it. The sticker price you are thinking of is what gets paid in the open market, and that is the market you simply avoid. You will never get the full sum, but what you do get is still a lot of money.

You might also be looking at it as a plain larceny when it was planned as insurance fraud. In that version you stage the taking, collect the payout from the carrier, and that is the end of the matter. The fact that the thing eventually turns up does not necessarily undo the cash that already changed hands. You might well have gotten the entire claim amount out of the scheme before anyone looked for the instrument again.

You're imagining a single rich person walking in and buying the thing. That's not how it works. You break the chain of ownership into a dozen or more small transactions across different countries. Each handler takes a cutting and passes it along with a fresh, wholly false story about the instrument's history. By the time it gets to a final buyer, the "famous" origin has been buried under so many layers of invented provenance that it's effectively a different object. The fame doesn't stop the process, it just makes the end product easier to mark up.

You can also take it apart. The scroll on an old fiddle is often a piece of boxwood that's been worked into something very hard to replace. The end button, the fittings, even the varnish have value to a restorer. You've got a bunch of very hard to trace components that can be sold to specialists.

And in a fair number of cases the whole thing is just an insurance play. You stage a theft, the payout comes in, and the instrument either gets quietly returned or is discarded. Nobody in the scheme is trying to resell the thing at all.

The "anyone would recognize it" part is also a bit overblown. A label in the sound hole or an inscription on the back doesn't mean every middleman in a long transshipment route is going to cross reference it against a missing property list. Plenty of people in the trade just take the story they're given.

You don't need to sell it to the people who'd recognize it. You need one buyer, in one market that doesn't check very carefully. There's a whole shadow tier of the instrument trade, particularly in a few countries, where provenance questions get waved through. The thing has to get past one person's skepticism, not the awareness of the whole world. You can also cut your losses by selling off the fittings and fittings, or just waiting for the identification to fade in public memory.

There's also the angle that you aren't trying to get the full value out of it. Forcing the original owner to buy it back from you for a small fraction of its worth is a pretty common endgame. You've made a few hundred grand and the owner has absorbed a much larger hit. The fact that this one got found might say more about how hard it is to get a single person to wire six figures in cash for a known stolen object than it does about the object being impossible to move. You'd probably get further with a slightly less legendary name on the label.

You're mostly right that it kills the option of selling it to a serious buyer. The whole scheme depends on time. You get the thing out and move it to some far off country, where an inside contact will pass it along to a buyer. By the time the original owner gets a trail to follow the strings are tangled enough that nobody can sort them out. The item being famous just forces you to be more careful, it doesn't make the job impossible.

Then there's the matter of you stealing your own insurance policy. You yank the thing, you collect the check, you put the violin back a month or two later. Everybody ends up whole except the insurer.

And let's not forget that a certain very narrow set of people will pay you a great deal of respect for even trying. The violin ends up back on the shelf, sure, but you've already banked a bit of legend. That's worth something to the right sort of person.

You just don't sell it to anyone who's in the know. The whole game is shoving it off to some middleman in a different country, or telling a gullible collector a made up history. That link in the chain doesn't need to know it's the 1715 Exeter violin. They just need to think it's a nice old Italian job. You can also wait a few years for the whole thing to get buried under a pile of new stories. The fact that it's so famous actually works in your favor. It means a fence is almost certain to get a very large return on it. That return is going to be much less than a million, sure, but it's still a lot of money.

Most of the time you aren't trying to bring the thing back to the light of day in the first place. You just need to get it far enough away from the people who remember where it was supposed to be. That's how it gets done with paintings and rare books too. The notoriety you're worried about is only a barrier if you're foolish enough to be open about it.

You'd be surprised how much of the art world runs on private, off the record deals. Nobody is going to try to move a thing like that on an open market. It goes from one private hand to another with a forged history to back it up. You make up a plausible if unverifiable past for the thing and it can in fact get sold at auction. The instrument gets a whole new identity. You only need a single counterparty who is content not to check the paperwork too closely.

There's also a pretty straightforward ransom angle to it. You don't need to get rid of the thing at all. You just need to prove you have it in a way that convinces the owner to pay. The fact that it ended up getting returned is pretty much consistent with some deal getting made behind closed doors.

You are picturing a single world where everyone has the same perfect information. It is a lot more full of back rooms than that.

groups.question: The world can't agree on standard units of measurement for anything except time. H ow come?
texts:
You've mostly got it because you can't fake time. A second is a second in every timezone, so nobody needs to vote on it. You don't need a committee to agree that the sun comes up. Try to do that with a foot or a pound and you run into a pretty nasty problem. You have to pick out some physical thing, a bar of metal say, and get everyone to accept it. The French wanted that bar to be based on the size of the Earth. The British were in no hurry to go along.

You end up with a bunch of local systems that work well enough for the people using them. Switching costs are just too high to be worth it. You'd have to retool everything and retrain a lot of people. The metric system did eventually take over most of the world but that was a process that stretched out over more than a century. The US is still sort of holding out on it. It's less that there's some deep intellectual disagreement and more that nobody wants to pay the price of getting around it.

It's mostly an accident of what you can see from a hilltop. The sun getting out of your hair is such a reliable event that every tribe ended up with the same basic day. You just had to split that up and the parts happened to get copied around. You never hit on anything quite as obvious for length. There's no natural stick that everyone can see from anywhere, so every kingdom went ahead and made up its own. You got a lot of the world to switch over to the metric system later on. Too late for the UK and the US though. They were so used to their old way of doing things that they just kept on with it.

You can't get off the hook so easily with time either. Try to sell some goods by a privately defined hour and you'd be caught out in a jiffy. You have a bit more room to fudge the length of a board or the size of a piece of land.

You mostly got there, you've just maybe left out a few details. The meter and the kilogram are the official international standards, and scientists and importers use them pretty much everywhere. The old feet and pounds are what you see in daily life in a couple of places, mostly on the basis of habit.

You need a common sense of when things are going to happen to get any of your other business done. If you're going to send goods some distance you have to be able to agree on a loading date and a payment date. That pressure to agree on a shared time scale is a lot more immediate than any pressure to agree on what a unit of weight should be. You can get along fine with local conventions on the latter so long as you only trade in your own area.

You also got some of the way you are in with the sexagesimal way of dividing up the day. That system got so thoroughly worked into the habits of the people who happened to be doing the most long distance trading. By the time those long range connections got to be very important it was already the thing everybody was using.

You mostly get it by accident. You all get the same sun to rise and set on, and that hands you a shared day for free. You've never had a ready made reference like that for the length of a foot or the weight of a stone. You've just kept inventing your own.

And the cost of getting it wrong is very different. If you and I use different weights to trade, we can huddle over a scale and work out a price. It's a headache but we get there. If our train schedules run on different days the train simply never comes to meet you. That kind of breakdown is far more immediate and painful to熬 out. People end up forcing a single rule for time out of plain necessity. They never felt the same kind of pressure to sort the rest out.

That said you are a bit off on the idea that time is the only shared rule. A fair share of the long distance trading routes forced a common set of weights and measures on the people using them. It just never got pushed out to the whole of the world the way the shared day did.

You've mostly got it backwards. Almost the whole planet has gotten together on the metric system for length and weight. You're up against the U S, Liberia and Myanmar keeping the old english system alive, and even the U S uses metric for anything in science. Its mostly just the trouble of switching that has kept the old thing around. Time is the one thing you can't really change. You have to count off the day by the earth's rotation and the year by its trip around the sun. You can't just get together and decide to use a shorter day. You have to take what the sky gives you. That fixed set of facts is the only part that everyone ends up with.

You mostly can. The US, Liberia and Myanmar are the big holdouts on the metric system and even they use it in science and medicine. You just get tripped up by the groceries. Time is the one thing you couldn't get away with fudging. You can't argue with the sun coming up and going down, or the seasons changing. Every culture looked up and saw the same clock running overhead. You can make up your own idea of what a foot or a pound is, but you can't change the length of a day.

You've also got a lot of neck to break on the other measures. It costs a fortune to swap out every ruler and scale that a country has accumulated over the years. With a clock you can just agree on what the next chime means and move on.

You've got it partly backwards. We do have a pretty clear international agreement on length and weight. The metric system is the official standard in every country except the US, Liberia, and a few of the Caribbean islands. Most of the disagreement you run into is just the US refusing to change over. The cost of reprinting every sign and rebuilding every machine is pretty hard to swallow.

It's a lot easier to get a handle on the second than on the foot or the pound. You can define a second by the super steady vibrations of a particular atom. You can't get that same kind of neat, unchangeable basis for the others. So even where the official rules are the same the old habits keep getting in the way.

You've mostly got it backwards. The world actually does agree on a pretty complete set of units for length, mass, volume, and the rest. That's the metric system. The US, Liberia, and a handful of others are the main holdouts, and they mostly use the old British imperial set. Everyone else has more or less got on board. Time is just the one thing where even those holdouts use the same scheme.

You have a bit of a built in advantage there. You can't really standardize the length of a day or a year since the planet sets those for you. The only part to get sorted out was how to chop those up, and the old base 60 system from the Babylonians was so deeply baked in to astronomy that nobody either managed or bothered to replace it. Navigation made it practically mandatory for ships to be on the same clock.

With your rods and your balances the situation was more of a mess. You had to pick between some dozens of local traditions that had real commercial interests behind them. You ended up with a winner, but it got in a lot of places a lot more slowly.

groups.question: why is my school so sensitive to religion amongst students, but also purposely doesn't serve meat on Fridays?
texts:
You are mostly getting two different rules that happen to have the same religious root. The menu thing is the school running its own house rules, the same way a Jewish day school would bake matzo into the snack lineup. Nobody is pretending that is a neutral choice. The fuss you are seeing over student expression is the school trying to keep from teaching any one dogma to kids of other faiths that happen to be in the building. A public school has to steer much more widely clear of all of that, a private one just has to keep its own signposts pretty well hidden.

You probably are not getting the religious part of the Friday thing because it is so old. It has been around long enough to start to look like a random tradition. That is kind of the whole point of how these places get away with it. They don't have to be any less religious, they just have to be a little more discreet about where that religion is coming from.

You're almost certainly at a Catholic school. The whole thing is built on a line they've drawn for a long time. They figure that abstaining from meat on Fridays is a general moral habit worth inculcating in every kid, the same way you'd insist on telling the truth or not stealing. Prayer, mass, and the more explicitly doctrinal stuff they've decided to leave to your own family. You don't have to actually believe in the thing for them to make you go along with the habit.

That said you're not wrong that it gets weird. The Friday rule is as specifically Catholic as the rosary is. You've just got a bunch of people who've decided that one is more of a good habit to teach in a general education setting. They've been getting away with that distinction for a while now. You'll find the same sort of thing at a lot of old religious schools that have to operate in a public framework.

The rules have also been pretty loosely enforced in most places for the last twenty or thirty years. You might be getting a stiffer version of the whole thing than your older siblings did.

You are probably running up against two different legal requirements that look like a double standard. The no meat thing is almost certainly a health or environmental policy, or maybe just a habit that got kept around. The fact that it lines up with the Catholic abstinence rule doesn't make it a religious endorsement. Schools are allowed to make that kind of choice on secular grounds. You would not be allowed to do the same thing for the sabbath, though, since that would singl out a specific group.

That second rule is what gets in the way of student religious activity. If the school let students get together to pray or proselytize it would be taking a side. You can't get around that as long as the school is supposed to stay officially neutral. So it ends up looking as if the school is cracking down on one side of the issue while quietly pushing the other. It is really just trying to keep its hands off the whole thing in both directions.

It's probably just old habit. A lot of public schools in areas that used to be mostly Catholic kept the Friday fast going long after the student body got mixed up. You end up with a menu that's religious in its origin but officially gets passed off as just a tradition. It's kind of like how some of those places will still put a nativity scene up in the lobby. Nobody wants to make a fuss over it so it just keeps getting repeated. If you got the food service people to talk they'd almost certainly tell you it's what the kids are used to. They'd be very careful to say it had nothing to do with any religious rules.

You might get a little more out of the district's own history. If you can dig up when the rule got started you'll see the old parish schools getting absorbed into the public system and the practice getting carried right along with them. That's the whole story in most cases.

You're running into the whole "general dietary accommodation" loophole. The fish thing almost certainly got grandfathered in a long time ago, and nobody ever had to write "this is for the Catholics" on the menu. It just reads like a menu choice anyone might make. That invisible quality is what keeps it from getting caught by the same rules that stop a kid from praying in the hallway. If they did the same trick with, say, lamb every day of Ramadan, it would probably get through just as easily.

You'd get a pretty similar result if you looked at the medical exemption side of things. A bunch of religious observances get folded in there too, and they stop getting flagged because nobody has to say the word religion. The rules you are seeing aren't so much a double standard as they are a single standard that happens to have a very lopsided way of getting around itself. You just happen to be noticing the part that got through the net.

You're seeing two different rules get applied to two different things. The Friday thing is the school's own identity getting baked into the schedule. If it's a Catholic school they can totally build their whole week around the abstinence tradition. That's them being themselves. The sensitivity to you is a legal constraint. They aren't allowed to advance or get in the way of any particular religion in how they treat the kids. They can't say you have to be Catholic, but they also can't say you can't be something else. You're sort of allowed to practice your own stuff so long as the school doesn't get behind it. The whole setup is just the institution being free to be a church while simultaneously being forbidden to act like one toward you.

That said you might be misreading the first part a bit. If they are acting pretty touchy about you it may be that some of your stuff brushes up on the things they need to keep out. It's hard for them to tell the line exactly and they've got a lot to lose if they get it wrong. So they tend to err on the side of not touching the subject at all.

You're seeing two different rules that happen to trip over each other. The part that stops you from talking about your faith is there to keep the school from getting dragged into a lawsuit. The Friday thing is just an old habit they've never gotten around to fixing. It's a lot easier to keep an old tradition than it is to pick out which new opinions to allow. They almost certainly don't think of the meatless lunch as having anything to do with the fast it originally came from. To them it's just the way the menu has always been.

You aren't going to get a straight answer if you push on it. You'll just be told that one rule is about keeping the peace and the other is purely a matter of custom. Both of those statements are a little bit of a dodge but they are the only ones you are likely to get.

It's almost certainly a leftover from when the place was run by a Catholic order. You see it in tons of old Jesuit and Franciscan schools that have since had to open up to everyone. Nobody ever got around to changing the menu because it was cheap and the whole place was used to it. That habit has nothing to do with what students are allowed to believe or say.

The rules you run into with student expression come from the law. The whole place has to keep from looking like it endorses any one faith. You can't make a religious fast into an official school thing without getting in trouble for that. You are basically looking at a set of civil rules colliding with a bunch of old traditions that nobody has bothered to sort out. You will find the same weird double standard in a lot of places that used to be fully religious.

groups.question: when commercials say "Next 20 callers will receive..." How do they keep track of that?
texts:
You've got a bank of lines all routed to the same counter. That counter is just an integer that goes up each time a call gets through. The moment it hits 20 the switch cuts off the prize path and you get a recorded message saying it's over. You definitely get some people with auto dialers hammering the thing, and the sponsors know that's coming. It's why the prize is almost always something you could get for a few dollars. They'd lose more in shipping a real prize than they'd get back.

The order you get in is the order in which the connections actually complete. Not the order in which you hit the send key. So you could be the first to push the button and still be twenty fifth to get through. None of that is particularly hard to set up on the kind of switches they use. It works about as well as a hotel front office counting off the last few rooms.

It's mostly just a dumb counter. The system that picks up the call has a little variable it checks before it plays the recording. If that variable is under 20 it says you won and takes your order. If it's 20 it plays the sorry we're fully subscribed message. You bump that variable up by one each time a call gets through. They don't really bother to check if it's the same person calling again. texts:
It's mostly the thing you have to show before you can get anything else. You can't get a driver's license or a passport without one, and the same holds true for getting married or having a baby. Banks will also make you produce it to open an account. When you go to get a job they'll want to see it to verify you are who you say you are and old enough to work. It is also the only record you'll have to prove who your parents are, which is a pretty big deal if it comes to wills or custody. If you ever get into the snafu of having to change your name the whole process still starts from that original record.

You probably won't actually carry it around with you that much once you are older. Once you have your license and passport to fall back on the original stays locked away in a safe or a file cabinet. You only ever need to dig it out to get a replacement for one of those.

You run into it on a lot of fronts. You can't get a driver's license or a state ID without one, and no passport either. You'll have to produce it to get married. It's what you show to get on the voter roll. Banks and other lenders look at it to be sure of who you are. It also figures in any court case that has to sort out your family status. Pretty much every other official paper you'll ever get gets checked back against it.

You do run into a few gray areas. Some places will let you get a state ID with a couple of secondary documents, and a few religious organizations will perform ceremonies without seeing it. But once you want to get any of those ceremonies or IDs officially recognized you are back to needing that original paper.

It's the one thing everything else keys off of. You'll need it to get a driver's license or a passport, and you can't vote without one. You can't get married, open a bank account, or sign a long term lease without showing it either. Kids can't get into school without it and your family will need it to sort out your estate when you die. You pretty much can't function as a legal person in the US or most other countries without it.

The only time you'll really notice how much depends on it is when you lose it. groups.question: How did the commonality of "seeing the light" originate when people are "crossing over" or passing away?
texts:
You've got two things getting mixed up here. The medical version says your visual cortex is just having a meltdown. When the brain gets starved of oxygen it starts to randomly fire off the same way it does in a dream or a hallucination. Since a sharp, bright point of stimulation is something your eyes know really well, your brain fills in that gap with a very convincing beam. That happens the same way to people who are having a seizure or taking certain drugs. So the raw event is pretty mundane.

What you are mostly running into is the story those people have already stored in their heads. You don't get a universal light you get a universal story. Christians end up seeing a gateway to heaven while people from other backgrounds see something that fits their own set of expectations. The whole thing got cemented in the popular imagination by a couple of psychologists in the nineteen seventies who insisted they had found a universal pattern in all that very diverse testimony. They pretty much invented the modern version of the experience.

It's mostly a matter of what happens to the brain when it's starved of oxygen. The occipital lobe at the back of the head handles your vision, and when it gets short changed it can start throwing off bright phosphenes. You get something similar when you rub your eyes. On top of that the parietal lobe, which builds your sense of where your body is in space, starts to malfunction. You end up feeling like you are viewing the scene from the outside. Stimulation of that area in the lab reproduces the effect pretty faithfully.

Your brain is also pumping out massive quantities of endorphins and a few other chemicals in that situation, and those produce their own set of vivid and highly pleasurable sensations. So you have a bright spot plus a strong sense of being removed from your body plus a deep feeling of peace.

The rest of the story is mostly your own head filling in the blanks. You see a tunnel because you've heard tunnels in these stories before. You see your dead grandmother because she is someone you wanted to see. You get the same broad outline in a lot of different cultures, which points to a shared underlying set of brain mechanisms. The specific characters and details differ to match whatever that culture has ready to go. Nobody has a complete account of the whole thing yet.

You're mostly getting your brain misfiring at you. When blood flow to the head gets cut off the visual cortex starts to generate things on its own. That ends up looking like a bright spot at the end of a tunnel. You get a very similar effect from rubbing your eyes or from having your pupils constricted. You are literally watching the internal activity of your own visual machinery. You can also get the whole thing by zapping the relevant part of the cortex with electricity. Certain drugs that mess with the visual pathway will do it too.

Where that stops being physiology and starts being religion is up to the person having the experience. The brain hands over the raw perception and the person's existing set of beliefs fills in the rest. Someone brought up on one set of ideas will read the event one way, and someone else will read it another.

The particular wording you are hearing about isn't that old. The whole crossing over conceit got into the popular sense mostly through 18th and 19th century religious writing. Before that you don't see the two ideas so neatly paired off in the same way. People were reporting the light for a long time before that vocabulary was around to dress it up.

There isn't really one origin you can point to. You've got the old religious stuff that's been around for a couple of millennia. The New Testament has the good thief on the cross getting a bright welcome, and plenty of other traditions have their own glowing version of what's on the other side. Those stories get worked into the local picture of what happens. Then in the twentieth century you get doctors and researchers like Raymond Moody collecting lots of first person reports from people who'd been clinically dead. Moody's 1975 book was a huge best seller and it sort of lumped all the different reports together and presented them as one universal event. That did a lot to make the light seem like some basic feature of the human brain.

You probably can't get to the raw sensory experience underneath all the cultural coating though. People seem to fill in the details with whatever their own background tells them to expect. A christian is going to see angels, someone else is going to see something quite different. The light itself may well be the brain doing something in an oxygen deprived state but the story that gets grafted on top of it is entirely local. So the commonality is mostly an artifact of the way the reports have been collected and told.

You've got a mix of biology and old storytelling there. On the biology side, cutting off blood to the brain knocks the visual cortex out in a pretty particular way. You end up with a bright spot that works its way in from the edges, which looks a lot like a tunnel with a light at the end. The temporal lobe gets into the act too and can pump out these very convincing hallucinatory experiences. Add in the fact that you are apparently in a state of extreme stress and your brain is trying to make some sense of the whole thing.

The stories you are hearing have been around far longer than we have had any way to explain them. Christians have their good shepherd, the ancient Egyptians had their own version of a guiding light, and a dozen other cultures got in on the act. People have always been too handy at reading their own neurology as the work of the divine to pass up the chance. The light you get from a dying brain just happened to fit the afterlife narratives they had already built up.

It's mostly a trick of the visual cortex. When your heart stops or you otherwise get a bad cut off of blood, the center of your visual field goes dark while the edges stay lit. The brain has a ready made interpretation for that pattern: a dark passage with a bright spot at the far end. You can get something pretty close to it by applying the right sort of electrical stimulation to the visual cortex. Layer on top of that the fact that a failing brain has a much harder time filtering out random neural noise, and you end up with a pretty vivid and emotionally charged vision.

The *story* you wrap around that vision is where your own culture gets in. A medieval Englishman is going to see angels, a Hindu will see something quite different, and so on. You get the same basic visual event with a very different set of characters and plot.

One small wrinkle is that these are reports from people who were resuscitated. Nobody who is actually gone has gotten back to give an account, so the whole thing is, strictly speaking, an account of what the dying brain does rather than what the dead one sees. Whether that simple blood flow story gets at the whole of the experience is still something people argue about. The emotional weight people take away from it seems to outrun the visual mechanics.

You've got a couple of different things braided together there. The deepest one is the Christian heaven as a place of literal brightness. The Book of Revelation has a City of God with no need of a sun because its light is God, and a whole lot of medieval and renaissance painting went with that. You get the idea of a soul going up into that radiance. That's the part that's really old.

The river crossing is a separate and also very old image. The Egyptians had the dead get rowed across to the afterlife, the Greeks put the Styx between the living and the dead, and you find variants all over the place. So the person is getting on a boat to get to that bright place on the far side. "Crossing over" is just the river part of that whole picture.

What you most likely have in mind, the tunnel and the light at the end, is a much newer layer. Patient reports of that started to get collected and published in the 1970s and 80s. Some neurologists have suggested the tunnel effect comes from the visual cortex starting to drop out from the outside in when blood flow fails, but that's still pretty much a best guess. The reports got so wide that they ended up confirming the older religious picture in people's minds.

You won't find a single date where all that got welded into the set of phrases you hear today. It just kept getting added to.

You've got a few separate things that ended up with the same label. The tunnel part is mostly a known quirk of how your eyes and optic nerve work. You already have a blind spot on the inside of your visual field, and the whole thing is somewhat tubular to begin with. Drop the blood supply to your brain and the outside of that field goes dark first. You wind up staring down a tube. That happens to people who are fainting or in shock and they have no religious framework to hang the experience on.

The bright light at the far end is a little trickier. It's probably your visual cortex firing off on its own once it stops getting real input from the eyes. You see the same sort of thing in people who have lost their sight and start seeing very vivid phantoms. The brain is just making up pictures. Where the picture goes from there is down to what stories you were handed. Christians, Muslims, and Hindus all report a light, but each group has a very different idea of what that light is for.

So the commonality you're asking about is mostly a matter of very similar brains getting very similar raw material and then dressing it up in whatever local mythology was already on file.

You're getting two different numbers depending on what you mean. The electrons you are actually pushing around the wire crawl along at maybe a fraction of an inch per second. That is about as fast as you would push a pond of marbles by adding one at an end. What gets a light bulb to come on almost instantly is a change in the electromagnetic field. That change races down the wire at roughly 50 to 99 percent of the speed of light. The exact figure for that part depends mostly on the kind of insulation you have wrapped around the conductor.

It is the same sort of thing as a long tube already full of water. If you force one drop in at the top it looks like a drop comes out the bottom immediately. In reality the drop you forced in is going to take a隆隆 very long time to get there.

It depends on what you mean by the word. The electrons themselves are pretty much at a standstill, drifting along at a fraction of a millimeter per second. That's the same thing you get in a line of billiard balls when you shoot the one at the end. The energy and the signal is what zips down the line, and it gets there at a good 50 to 99 percent of the speed of light. You get the higher end of that range in a coaxed cable and a bit less in a standard building wire. In a vacuum you can get the electrons themselves to go pretty close to that top off speed, but you are never actually going to hit it.

So if you are wondering why the light in the next room comes on the instant you flip the switch the answer is that the energy transfer is almost as fast as a ray of light. The individual particles doing the work are not.

You've got two different things going on. The signal that tells the whole circuit to light up moves at most a little under 200,000,000 meters per second. That's the electromagnetic field propagating down the wire, and it's close to the speed of light. You will see a light turn on almost instantly even on a very long circuit.

The electrons themselves are a different story. In a copper wire carrying a normal current they are drifting along at something like a millimeter or two per second. It would take them many days to go from the switch to the light. None of that slow crawling gets in the way of the much faster field that carries the effect.

You'd get different field speeds in different insulators. Solid dielectrics will slow it down more than air does. You are probably most familiar with the 2/3 of light speed figure that comes out of the plastic jacket on common coaxial cable.

You'd only get a different answer if you got into some special case like superconductors, and that's probably not what you are after. The "almost the speed of light" number is the one that actually matters in practice.

groups.question: Why are death row inmates housed separately?
texts:
It's mostly about keeping the legal process from getting messed up. You've got people with absolutely no reason to try to get out except to avoid the end result, so the chances of a sharp escape attempt are a lot higher. And you've got people on the outside who might try to get in to kill them or otherwise stop the courts from getting to a final result. Shoving them into a small tightly controlled group makes both of those much harder to pull off. The courts have been pretty clear that the whole thing needs to happen in an environment free from that kind of outside interference.

You also get a bit of a practical benefit in that you don't have to worry about them getting killed by other people on the inside. That last point cuts both ways though, since the environment it creates is so damn isolating you end up with a whole new set of legal problems.

It comes down to keeping a small group from helping one another get out. You can't do that if they're mixed in with the general population. It is just easier to put a dozen or two dozen people in a fortified unit than to keep an eye on them everywhere else. You also have to keep that group from the wider public so nobody on the outside can get in and help. That last part is what makes the whole thing so isolating. The psychological damage that comes from it is pretty much an unavoidable side effect of the way you have to set it up.

You'll see the exact details vary from state to state. Some places put them in separate buildings while others just set off one wing of a larger facility. You might also find that the facilities are a lot more spartan than you would get in the general population since you are only housing so few of them.

You mostly get the security and legal reasons. You can't have the rest of the population gang up on a guy, and you can't let him get to a judge to try to stay the execution. Appeals also take a really long time, sometimes decades, so you need a place to keep him that is out of the way. A few states have gotten out of the strict solitary thing by using protective custody units that let you get out of a cell for a while. That doesn't really get at the moral questions of the whole setup though, and those have been fought out in the courts for years.

You will find that the courts have mostly refused to get involved with the day to day of those units. The arguments about whether long term isolation amounts to a form of torture have not gotten very far as far as actually changing the way the places are run. You are looking at a system that was mostly put together to keep the process from being interfered with.

You've got to keep them from getting together. That's the whole game. In a group they could put together a coordinated plan to take a guard hostage or to get out. Or a guy who is about to be executed might get killed by the others if they think it'll help their cause. You can't let that sort of communication happen. It is just as much about the safety of the guards though. A handful of people can be overpowered far more easily than a well fortified cell. You can't spare the extra men to watch over them if they were mixed in with the rest.

You do end up paying a pretty steep psychological price for it. The isolation does a lot of damage to a person, and there is quite a bit of litigation that has come out of that. The system ends up tolerating that harm because it doesn't really have a better way of handling the security risk. None of it is out of any particular cruelty. It is just the only arrangement that keeps the rest of the institution from getting involved.

You mostly get security. You can't stick a high value target in the general population and expect the guards to watch them every minute. The whole thing needs a dedicated staff to track the inmate around the clock. You also have to keep them from any chance of getting out while the legal process drags on. That process can run for years and you need the arrangement to stay in some kind of status quo. Folding a person into a regular wing while their appeal is pending would just open up a bunch of new legal problems.

None of that is to say the setup doesn't wreck a person's head. You end up with a lot of documented psychological damage that you sort of have to look the other way on. The requirements are just too many to handle any other way. You end up with a whole separate wing to deal with all of it.

You mostly get to keep them from helping each other out. If you let a guy who is going to get away with it mix with the rest, he can pass on whatever dark ideas he has. You can't let the rest of the population get at him either since they might kill him while he is still working his way through the appeals. That last part is a huge one because you can't let a prisoner die before his lawyers get a chance to raise every point they can think of.

That legal tangle is what really drives the whole thing. You end up with a separate population that gets a separate and much more restricted way of life. That is the only way to keep the rest of the prison from getting slammed with all the civil rights suits that would otherwise be in the offing. The isolation is just what that legal situation forces you to do.

You've got a mess of legal and practical reasons tangled up. The most obvious one is that you can't keep a guy the state intends to put to death in the general population. The rest of the population would be in danger, and he'd be a target. You also need a place that's easy to keep under the kind of close watch that the endless appeals process demands. That process can drag on for decades and it wants a fairly fixed living arrangement to work from.

They also try to make the place a little more like a regular dorm than a solitary cell. That's because the total isolation that happens in the general prison setup would break most people. In practice it still ends up being pretty lonely though. You're stuck in that unit for a very long time with a very limited set of contacts.

It's mostly an appeals hassle. You've got to keep the person from getting into new legal trouble while the case works its way through the courts. Any fresh fight or incident hands the defense new stuff to get a stay or a new trial. You've also got to keep the rest of the prison from killing the person. If that happened the whole process would be out the window and you'd be back at square one.

You end up with a bunch of 22 or 23 hour solitary as a result. That part was never really meant to be a form of punishment, it just sort of grew up that way. Nobody wants to take the chance of mixing such a person in with the general population, so they get locked down. It has some pretty rough psychological effects on top of everything else.

groups.question: How people program "Angry Birds"-like physics and collision detection.
texts:
You are almost certainly going to outsource the whole thing to a library like Box2D or Chipmunk. Rolling your own impulse solver is a rabbit hole that eats months. These engines give you a world object you throw bodies at. You tag the birds and pigs as circles and the wood and ice as polygons. Every frame the engine integrates gravity and velocity for each body. It then runs through a brute force check to see which pairs are overlapping.

The math for two circles is just a distance check between their centers. If that distance is less than the sum of their radii you have a hit. You find the normal by normalizing the vector connecting the two centers. For a circle hitting a box you have to test the distance from the circle center to each of the box's edges and pick the closest one. That gives you the normal and the exact contact point.

Once you have the normal you calculate an impulse to stop the bodies from sinking into each other. That is a straight application of conservation of momentum along that normal line. You scale it by a restitution coefficient which is just the bounciness of the materials. You then apply that impulse to both bodies in opposite directions. The whole thing runs over several constraint iterations in a single frame to keep the towers from shaking apart. You also clamp out any velocity that drops below a tiny threshold to get things to settle.

You're almost always bolting together a library like Box2D rather than writing the math yourself. You make a static world for the ground and then pop in the pigs and the little houses. The catch is the engine will only take convex shapes, so any L or U piece has to be sliced into a bunch of simpler triangles. Pigs are usually just circles since that's fast to test and nobody notices the corners are missing.

The slingshot is a one line thing. You take the drag vector, scale it, and fire that out as the bird's initial velocity. That same vector gets integrated forward with a fixed time step to draw the dotted trajectory line you see while aiming. The line is a pure prediction and has no effect on what actually happens once you let go.

The fun part is entirely in the material numbers you hand the engine. A wood block needs a different density and a different amount of energy loss in a hit than a stone one. Get those wrong and the bird punches right through a tower that should have come down, or the structure holds out when it clearly shouldn't. You end up hours of play testing to get that mix to feel right.

You are almost certainly playing with Box2D. It is the default for this whole genre and it handles the circle versus polygon math for you. The slingshot is just a mouse joint. You hook the bird to the pivot point with that, let the player drag the joint to the new position, and then you destroy the joint on release. Box2D takes the stored stretch and applies it as an impulse. You don't have to calculate any of that by hand.

Getting the right feel is mostly a matter of faking it. You give the pigs and the fruit a very low density to make them fly far when they get hit. You also set a pretty high restitution on the birds so they will bounce off the slingshot frame. If you let the simulation run until everything is perfectly still the game will drag. You are much better off writing a check that forces the whole thing to end after the birds come to a reasonable rest.

You will run into problems with the circles getting stuck in the corners of the boxes. Bumping up the number of internal solver iterations helps but it eats up your frame time. In practice you just have to design the levels so that you are not asking the math to get out of an impossible position. The whole thing is a lot more about picking the right numbers to throw at the solver than it is about writing any new math.

You're almost certainly using a library like Box2D and not rolling the integration and contact resolution yourself. The library handles the fixed timestep loop which is the part you have to get right. You step the physics world at some rate like 120 times a second and then lerp the drawn positions between the last two states to keep the visuals smooth. That fixed step thing is non negotiable or you'll end up with velocities that depend on your frame rate.

Getting a reasonable list of pairs to check is where most of the performance lives. The broad phase is just a spatial hash or a sort on the X axis so you only test things that are near each other. The narrow phase then does the actual circle and polygon overlap tests. You won't be doing anything fancy or pixel perfect in there.

The slingshot part is just applying an impulse to the bird in the direction you pull. You aren't solving a ballistic equation in advance to get the flight path. The dotted line you see in the aim UI is you running some number of tiny physics steps into a throwaway world and drawing out the results. You do that every time the aim changes which is fine since it is just a handful of chickens.

The target structures are static or kinematic bodies you place in the world. You watch the magnitude of the impulse that ends up hitting them to decide if a pig has taken enough damage to be removed. That is the entire damage model for a lot of these games.

You are almost certainly going to use Box2D or maybe a little bit of the newer Jolt library. You feed it your level as a bunch of static shapes and then you let it kind of take over. The birds are just dynamic circles you give an initial velocity vector from the slingshot drag. That's really the whole launch mechanic. From there the engine is integrating gravity and rotation for you every frame.

The collision part is mostly a matter of how you describe the shapes. The pigs are circles, the wooden bits are rectangles, the pigs inside them are just more circles. You tag all of these with material types and you write a contact listener to fire off when two of them hit. That callback tells you the impulse of the hit and you use that to decide whether a plank should shatter or just get dented. That wood versus stone distinction everyone likes is nothing more than different damage thresholds you have coded in to that listener.

You could hack together a home grown version by checking line and circle intersections yourself and doing your own impulse math. You'll end up fighting a lot of edge cases that the established libraries have already gotten through though. That contact listener pattern is the part that tends to trip people up since it inverts the usual game loop you might expect.

You almost certainly aren't writing any of it from scratch. You drop in something like Box2D, which has been the workhorse for this genre for a very long time. You then describe your world in terms of bodies. The ground and fixed walls are static. The structures are a pile of static convex polygons bolted together. The birds are circles, which keeps the math in the narrow phase really cheap. You let the engine do the integration and constraint solving every frame.

The slingshot is where you get a little hands on. You attach a mouse joint or distance constraint to the bird and just update its target position as the player drags. Let go of that constraint on release and the bird already has the velocity that got it there. You haven't fired a projectile so much as you've let a constraint go.

The whole destructible block thing is mostly a matter of what you do in the collision callback. You look at the impulse that just hit a piece, compare it to some threshold, and if it's too much you yank that body out of the world. You then throw in a handful of smaller bodies that have collision turned off entirely, purely so they tumble around for a second before you clean them up. They cost you nothing in solver time since the engine ignores them.

The one part that still takes fiddling is getting the threshold values right. Too loose and the whole structure collapses from a clip of the bird. Too tight and you need to hit it with a full charge to get anything to happen. You end up just playing through a lot of levels and nudging those numbers.

You're almost certainly using Box2D, which is what the original game and a huge pile of imitators ran on. You hand it a description of your world and it takes over. The bird is a circle, the pigs are circles, the slingshot is a pair of static fixtures you constrain to. The whole wooden fortress is a collection of dynamic bodies you've arranged and then attached with revolute joints. You set a mass on each thing, some coefficient of restitution for the bounciness, and a bit of friction. After that the engine is doing the heavy lifting on its own.

The dotted line you see before you let go is not the physics engine guessing at the future. It is just you solving the projectile motion equations for a parabola, since up to that point there are no collisions to worry about. The second the bird gets released you give it that initial velocity and stop worrying, because from there the engine will take over in unpredictable ways.

You get all that satisfying tower toppling for free from the impulse calculations the engine does on every contact. The only thing you have to add on top is a bit of bookkeeping. You track the impulse each pig gets hit with, knock an equivalent amount off its health, and when that runs out you delete the body out of the world. That covers pretty much all of it.

You are almost certainly looking at Box2D underneath. It is the workhorse for this kind of 2D stuff. You feed it a world and then you call a step function at a fixed rate, say 1 60th of a second. The rendering side just lerps between the last two physics states so it looks smooth on your screen. That fixed timestep is the part people get wrong, they try to step the sim based on frame time and end up with weird tunneling.

The collision side is a two pass affair. You keep an axis aligned bounding box tree around everything to quickly throw out the vast majority of pairs. Only what that broad phase flags gets the real math done on it. For your birds and the pigs you are mostly dealing with circles. The wooden and stone structures are convex polygons. When that narrow phase finds a contact it hands back a list of points and normals.

From there an impulse solver sorts out the result. You have to manually set up what happens when things hit. You just check the magnitude of the impulse that got applied to a box and if it passes a threshold you mark the whole thing for deletion. That deletion pass happens after the solver has done its thing. All the slingshot action is just a custom joint that you remove at the moment you decide to fire.

You're almost certainly using Box2D, which is what the original game and a huge pile of imitators ran on. You hand it a description of your world and it takes over. The bird is a circle, the pigs are circles, the slingshot is a pair of static fixtures you constrain to. The whole wooden fortress is a collection of dynamic bodies you've arranged and then attached with revolute joints. You set a mass on each thing, some coefficient of restitution for the bounciness, and a bit of friction. After that the engine is doing the heavy lifting on its own.

The dotted line you see before you let go is not the physics engine guessing at the future. It is just you solving the projectile motion equations for a parabola, since up to that point there are no collisions to worry about. The second the bird gets released you give it that initial velocity and stop worrying, because from there the engine will take over in unpredictable ways.

You get all that satisfying tower toppling for free from the impulse calculations the engine does on every contact. The only thing you have to add on top is a bit of bookkeeping. You track the impulse each pig gets hit with, knock an equivalent amount off its health, and when that runs out you delete the body out of the world. That covers pretty much all of it.

The core is a physics engine, and almost everyone in this space uses Box2D. It's 2D, it's fast, and it handles the ragdoll-ish behavior you see up close. The engine works on a fixed timestep, though, so you're stepping the simulation at maybe 60 times per second and then interpolating for the display. That's why things can look smooth even though the math is happening in discrete jumps.

Collision detection is basically two layers. First you do a broad phase with bounding volumes that are cheap to test, usually an AABB tree. Then you only run the expensive narrow phase tests on pairs that the broad phase flags. For the birds and pigs you're dealing with circles and convex polygons almost exclusively. The narrow phase then gives you the contact points you need.

You handle the rest with impulse based constraint solvers. That's what lets a bird smash through a wooden box and keep going. You just set the destruction threshold on the box and mark it for removal when that impulse gets too high. The whole thing is a pretty tight loop of stepping the physics, checking damage, and cleaning up.

You are almost certainly looking at Box2D underneath. It is the workhorse for this kind of 2D stuff. You feed it a world and then you call a step function at a fixed rate, say 1 60th of a second. The rendering side just lerps between the last two physics states so it looks smooth on your screen. That fixed timestep is the part people get wrong, they try to step the sim based on frame time and end up with weird tunneling.

The collision side is a two pass affair. You keep an axis aligned bounding box tree around everything to quickly throw out the vast majority of pairs. Only what that broad phase flags gets the real math done on it. For your birds and the pigs you are mostly dealing with circles. The wooden and stone structures are convex polygons. When that narrow phase finds a contact it hands back a list of points and normals.

From there an impulse solver sorts out the result. You have to manually set up what happens when things hit. You just check the magnitude of the impulse that got applied to a box and if it passes a threshold you mark the whole thing for deletion. That deletion pass happens after the solver has done its thing. All the slingshot action is just a custom joint that you remove at the moment you decide to fire.

groups.question: What makes the F-14 so loved and the F-35 so hated?
texts:
You're mostly looking at a story problem. The F 14 has a whole generation of guys who saw Top Gun and concluded that thing with the big moving wings was the apex of man. That movie basically wrote the aircraft into their personal mythology. You can see the wings sweep and it looks like it's doing something heroic. It's all definitely there for you to look at.

The F 35 got stuck with the opposite of all that. It's a shape that's specifically designed to not stand out, which to a casual observer just looks like some sort of overgrown SU 27. Then you pile on two decades of cost overruns and schedule slips and you've got a whole lot of material to take pot shots at. People in that community also genuinely prefer the idea of a specialist to this do everything in one package.

None of that has much to do with what the actual planes do in a fight. You've got a bunch of folks who've attached their feelings to the narratives they've been handed and they defend those narratives pretty fiercely. Change the story and the feelings change right along with it.

Most of it is just Top Gun. That movie welded a really sexy image of the Tomcat to a bunch of people's brains. You get the variable sweep wings, the long pointy nose, the whole lone gunslinger cowboy thing. The F 35 was designed to be hard to see on radar which means it ended up looking like a lumpy flying briefcase. It just does not have the same romantic appeal.

That said the hate is also about the program the plane sits in. The thing has been late and way over budget for what feels like a decade. When a project keeps missing its own targets people start lashing out at the object itself. You end up with a pile of reliability jokes that are really about the management mess around them. You are basically comparing a really well oiled legend to a very long and often frustrating real world development effort.

You've got two planes that are both pretty terrible to keep flying, but they got wildly different reputations. Top Gun did more for the Tomcat than any actual air to air victory ever could. You got a great looking bird with a variable sweep wing and a guy in a cool leather jacket doing tricks with it. That made an entire generation of guys decide the thing was a war machine. The F 35 came in without that kind of fiction already wrapped around it. It also got caught in a procurement nightmare where every single bug got reported to the press. The plane is probably getting better as the software gets fixed, but nobody is going to write a movie about that.

You are also watching the old one with the benefit of a lot of time to smooth out the edges. Nobody talks about the Tomcat eating its own mechanics or the fact that it needed a whole lot of people to get it in the air. People remember the movie and forget the maintenance logs. The new plane is still in the middle of its growing pains with the whole country looking over its shoulder. It will likely end up being a pretty good aircraft in the end, but that story will never get the same kind of screen time.

It's mostly a matter of when you got to see them. The Tomcat had Top Gun to put it on a screen for a couple hundred million people. That movie showed off a plane that looked like it walked out of a comic book, all long nose and big swinging wings. You could see the six gun pod out on a pylon too. There was something you could point at. That generation of pilots also got to fly a two man crew, pilot and radar intercept officer, which had a kind of old time charm. All of it is now safely in the past so you can look back on it without the current mess getting in the way.

The Lightning you are watching get built in public. You see the cost overruns and the schedule slips in the newspapers every few months. The whole thing was set up to be a single plane for four different branches which it never quite managed to be. It is also deliberately shaped to be hard to see, which does not make for a very stirring picture. Nobody can look at it and immediately get a sense of what it can do. You end up watching a very large software problem get worked out and that has a hard time inspiring much in the way of affection.

You are mostly just remembering them at different stages of life. You got to see the Tomcat in its prime, long after the teething problems got sorted out. That is the version that made it into the movies and the novels. You got to watch the Joint Strike Fighter get born in public. That process was a long, expensive, and often embarrassing exercise in bug fixing. It is a lot harder to write a pretty story about a software patch than it is to write one about a XML jet.

The Tomcat was also a brute. It could do one thing and do it with a kind of raw force that is easy to get worked up about. The new bird is trying to be a bunch of different things at once. That sort of all purpose complexity is almost guaranteed to produce the sort of rough edges that end up in the press. It isn't so much that one is good and the other is bad, you just got a front row seat to the good parts of one and the bad parts of the other.

Mostly it's that the Tomcat is a finished story and the Lightning is still being written. You got to look back at the F 14 from a safe distance and romance the whole thing. The variable sweep wing is just such a dramatic thing to look at, and the big Phoenix missiles made for an easy to understand identity. Throw in Top Gun and you have a pretty good legend. Nobody has to watch the software bugs get squashed or the cost get added up.

You are watching all of that happen in real time with the 35. It is also a lot harder to get worked up about a bird that is meant to do a little of everything. It does not have that one big visual hook to latch onto. You end up nit picking the thing that is still in front of you while you worship the one that is safely in the museum. You would probably feel the same way about a lot of other things if the roles were reversed.

That said the 35 does have some pretty bad technical problems to knock down. You are not entirely making any of that up in your head.

It's mostly a matter of when you got to see each one. You got the Tomcat back in the 80s when it was still actually getting into scrapes. Then along came Top Gun to write it off to the side as some sort of noble warrior. By the time you started to get pissed at its maintenance issues it had already been shuffled into the boneyard. You can't get too worked up about a thing that isn't around any more.

The 35 is still out there kicking and waking up every morning to some new set of teething problems. You see it in the papers today and you are left to sort out the difference between a small snafu and some kind of systemic failure. That constant stream of bad news builds up a pretty grudging picture in people's heads. You aren't really hating the aircraft so much as you are the endless and terribly managed business of getting it to fly.

You're partly just looking at two very different stories. The F 14 got to be a hero in Top Gun before it ever flew in anger. That movie sold a picture of the plane that matched its actual look, big variable sweep wings and all. You could see what it was doing. The F 35 is mostly a bag of hidden sensors and software, which is a lot harder to get excited about. It also hadn't been around long enough to get saddled with a long list of cost overruns. That list has been the main thing feeding the bad reputation the newer bird has.

Most of the grumbling you hear isn't really about the plane. It's about the way the whole thing got bought. You don't get that same clear cut villain to get mad at with the old Tomcat. It just left the stage in time to keep its good name.
